speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: What is the motion?

subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
I will read the motion:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to further Canadian participation in the development of industries and undertakings in Canada, to increase Canadian participation in the ownership of undertakings in Canada, and generally to further the development of the resources and industries of Canada; and for such purposes to establish an investment company, to be called the Canada Development Corporation, with a share capital structure whereby the largest possible numbers of Canadians may directly and indirectly invest capital in and profit from the ownership of Canadian industries and undertakings and the development of Canada; to authorize the guarantee by Canada of certain obligations of the corporation; to provide for the approval by the Minister of Finance of issues of guaranteed obligations of the corporation; to provide that the total liabilities of the corporation outstanding at any time shall not exceed one thousand million dollars; and to provide further for other related and incidental matters.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
My point of order, Mr. Speaker, was not a request that you should read the whole motion. It was that under standing order 21(2) the calling of this motion merely means
that it is transferred to and ordered for consideration under government orders in the same or at the next sitting of the house. We do not debate it at this point, we just transfer it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
May I be permitted to call the attention of the hon. member to standing order 21(1), which reads as follows:
Government notices of motions for the house to go into a committee of the whole at the next sitting of the house when put from the Chair shall be decided without debate or amendment.
The next subsection reads:
(2) When any other government notice of motion is called from the Chair, it shall be deemed to have been forthwith transferred to and ordered for consideration under government orders in the same or at the next sitting of the house.
Is the motion carried?

subtopic: MEASURE TO INCREASE CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN INDUSTRIES AND UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Carried.

On the basis of this survey the wheat board has decided to raise the general delivery quota to 12 bushels per specified acre effective Monday, June 24, at nearly half the delivery points. The board will make every attempt to equalize quotas at that level throughout western Canada by the end of the crop year. I have also been informed that the wheat board will raise the quota on Durum wheat to 15 bushels per seeded acre.
Hon. members will appreciate that this quota level will enable the vast majority of producers to deliver all the grain they wish to deliver with the exception of Durum wheat. In the case of Durum wheat, production during the last crop year was at an all time high and, rather than congest the grain marketing facilities with supplies of Durum wheat far in excess of market requirements, the board has decided to limit the Durum quota to 15 bushels per seeded acre.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, June 19, consideration of the motion of Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nowlan.
(Translation) :

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that today's discussion on the budget will remain unforgettable because of some accompanying circumstances. As far as I am concerned, I have no intention of trying to raise a scandal where there is none. I would not in any way like to question the honesty and sincerity of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). Indeed, I think that there can be no [Mr. MacEachen.l
doubt in that respect. Neither would I like to create a scandal around the fact that the Minister of Finance may have some advisers or experts in attendance when preparing his budget. All I want to do is to point out that in the past, the Liberal party, to which the minister belongs, has probably been the political party in Canada which specialized more than any other in stirring up scandal where there was none, or to distort the truth as much as possible, while raising unjustified doubt. And, today, the Liberal party is caught at its own game. Indeed, it taught others well enough how to create a scandal, and that is why it has to bear the consequences today.
As far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we never wanted such a policy. We did not accept it in the past, when applied by the Liberals. Neither shall we accept it when the same happens at the expense of the Liberals, and the proof is that, just a few days ago, I did not hesitate a moment to give a chance to the Minister of Finance himself to clear up any doubt that might have existed, whereas some hon. members wanted to prevent him from explaining a point raised by the hon. member of Calgary North (Mr. Harkness).
Mr. Speaker, we think that politics should have higher standards. If the Minister of Finance is to be blamed for anything, it is not because he consulted some advisers, but because he chose the wrong ones. People realize it today, because we see that the Minister of Finance has to take out of his budget some proposals and even some words which the wrong advisers put in his mouth, so to speak.
What is most important is that today we are living some hours of great significance for our country, when it appears without doubt that Canada is ruled by a government which kowtows to international finance.
The Minister of Finance submits a budget. Afterwards, protest is raised by the humble folk everywhere, by those who are employed in house construction, in the production and sale of building materials. Indeed, the Minister of Finance stated himself that he received letters and telegrams of protest from all sorts of organizations and societies. But nobody bothered. Not a single answer has been received with regard to those protests. The legislation itself is not clear and nobody bothers to explain it. The little man is left in complete ignorance of the nature of that legislation and the way it will be administered.
But now we have protests flowing in from the president of the Toronto stock exchange and the president of the Montreal stock exchange, from the American under secretary of state, from investment brokers, from big

financiers, one of whom was named a while ago, from the president, vice president or director of a large Montreal brokerage house. They come from big men of finance, not from ordinary Canadian citizens who make up the majority of the people, but from big financiers in Canada and especially from outside Canada.
It did not take long, Mr. Speaker, just a few days. The present government and its finance minister bowed, accepted, gave way before the protests of the big financial interests and withdrew the legislation under which a 30 per cent tax was imposed on the sale of Canadian corporations' shares to foreign interests. Mr. Speaker, I say this is a serious matter.
We see that the very same man, Mr. Eric Kierans, who during the last election campaign went from one end of the country to the other, spreading lies, distorting the Social Credit doctrine the better to fight and destroy it, I repeat, distorting it and lying shamelessly the better to fight Social Credit, that same man who stood up for American financial interests at that time, paid a visit to the Minister of Finance and, just 12 or 15 hours later, the tax on the sale of Canadian shares to non-residents was cancelled and withdrawn from the budget. So, Mr. Speaker, I maintain it is a shame to bow like that before the big men of finance in this country.
Please note, Mr. Speaker, that they put on quite a show. The Minister of Finance seemed annoyed by the tone of Mr. Kierans' letter, but he accepted Mr. Kierans' claims. He said that Mr. Kierans was wrong, but he accepted his claims.
Here we witness the greatest performance, I would even say the best show of hypocrisy ever seen. The president of the Montreal stock exchange and the Minister of Finance seemed to have daggers drawn, but the latter bowed before the president of the Montreal stock exchange who is the direct link with the American financiers, as president of the Montreal stock exchange and the Canadian stock exchange. That is, Mr. Speaker, the situation.
Faced with facts, Mr. Speaker, as I said a few moments ago, I do not want to doubt the honesty and sincerity of the Minister of Finance. I believe him to be a gentleman, polite and amiable but after what happened I think that if he has any pride or decency, he will admit that it is his duty, today, to resign as Minister of Finance of Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire
When we see that the person responsible for controlling the budget bends and crawls before the big financiers, then, Mr. Speaker, in view of the circumstances, I think that he has no other alternative but to leave honourably the post which he now occupies. He will show greater courage and strength than he has in the last 24 or 36 hours, if he resigns those functions that require its incumbent to be much more Canadian than he has shown himself to be in these last hours.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would like now to get to the heart of the debate. First of all; I notice-and I will use the speech of the Minister of Finance himself-that there is nothing new under the sun.
One remembers very well that the Liberals, when they were in opposition-and, here, it is spelled out-were against railway subsidies with regard to freight rates. The Minister of Finance said:
The initial series of payments has continued since-
-and we have been forced to provide $20 million for this purpose in the present fiscal year.
Forced. What forced him, Mr. Speaker? One fact only: there is nothing new under the sun.
Then he added:
In light of the continuing confusion in railway matters, the previous government appointed a royal commission on transportation in 1959.
And there, it says:
The failure of the previous government to deal effectively with the railway question thus means that we are faced with special railway subsidies this year aggregating $70 million.
"We are faced with", as if this were an obligation. It is just that two governments, the two old parties, have always travelled the same road. There is nothing new under the sun-things go on as they were.
And that is not all, Mr. Speaker. Here are other examples:
I indicated when I tabled these estimates that we have been forced to bring forward for this budget the expenditure estimates prepared by the previous government.
Forced by what? There is always the same motive being invoked, and the more it changes, the more it remains the same.
And a little further on:

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire
An examination of the tax structure shows clearly that taxes are already very high, but that the revenue they produce continues to fall short of necessary expenditures.
And it still goes on-our tax structure "shows clearly that taxes are already very high". But taxes are increased again. The more it changes, Mr. Speaker, the more it remains the same. Going still further, I find other instances. I quote the Minister of Finance:
Taxes must provide revenue sufficient to allow an important step toward budgetary balance. And since the increased outlays under certain new programs will be tapered off or stopped in two or three years time, provision can also be made for some revenue of a non-recurring nature.
Now, he says-
While it would not be correct to describe any tax as being popular anywhere-
Those are the words of the Minister of Finance-
-it is the case that indirect taxes such as the sales tax are now regarded with more favour in quite a number of countries than in the past.
Exactly as it was before. There is an attempt to hide taxes so that they should go unnoticed, and that Canadians would swallow them more easily. It is all the same thing over again-the more it changes, the more it remains the same, Mr. Speaker.
I heard the Liberals, when they were in the opposition, complain about deficits, claiming it was a shame for the country when the Conservatives had deficits. But today I notice that we have a deficit of $585 million, not counting what will be added, since the 30 per cent tax on the sale of Canadian securities has been abolished. Formerly, we had deficits of $600 or $700 million, but this year we have one of $585 million. The more it changes, Mr. Speaker, the more it remains the same.
And further on we find this:
Our net cash requirements for 1963-64, both budgetary and non-budgetary-
And this will increase it even more-
-are thus estimated to be about $850 million.
This is worse than last year. Here, we may say that the more things change, the worse they get.
Mr. Speaker, I can go on and find in this budget endless facts which prove that the more it changes, the more it remains the same.
But, what we would have liked to see, for instance, is the carrying out of the Liberal platform, because it had some good points.

We see, among other things, that the Liberal party will see to it that there is full employment, Mr. Speaker. I received yesterday from the Minister of Labour a word, a letter or rather a message, about the employment and unemployment situation for the week ended May 18, 1963, that is 30 days after the beginning of the 60-day period. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, it ends today and I wish the Prime Minister a happy anniversary for his 60 days of decision, specially since he has not decided anything apart from increasing the taxes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I put a question to the hon. member for Lapointe?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would he be willing to grant them three days of grace?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would it bring some special sanctifying grace to the Canadians? I do not think so.
So, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals were talking-it is to be found at the very beginning of their platform-about full employment. Let us see what the situation is today: on May 19, 1962, that is a year ago, there were, according to statistics, 336,000 unemployed; on May 18, 1963, there were 346,000 unemployed or 10,000 more.
We should have liked to see the platform of the Liberal party carried into effect but we see the reverse. And what else do we see? "Slums clearance to make room for better houses".
The Minister of National Revenue said: We shall give $500 to everyone who builds a home during the winter months, while we know that in winter the cost is increased by more than $500. The following day or a few days after, the Minister of Finance announces his tax.
Now, Mr. Speaker, here are some figures to show if the Minister of Finance with his tax has really encouraged home building and the clearance of slums. I have before me a book which I received yesterday morning, in English only, from the dominion bureau of statistics, which comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I have not received the French version. It bears the catalogue No. 64002. I only have it since yesterday. It points out that in 1962, 104,279 houses were built; at $500 per house, it comes to $52,139,500.
Now, the Minister of Finance expects that by adding his tax on building materials during the six remaining months of this year, it

would yield $170 million, which for a complete year, that is for 1964-1965, it would bring in $365 million and he would only have to spend $52 million.
He is actually taking back seven times more than what he is giving us. That is exactly the opposite of what was announced in the program of the Liberal party. It is not through such action that the Minister of Finance will promote home building.
Mention was also made in that program of improved health care. However, the matter is not even mentioned in the budget. This is what we would have liked to find there, but it is exactly the opposite that happens.
There had been some talk about increasing to $75 the allowances paid to blind and disabled persons. Yet, no such reference is made in the budget. We had been promised an increase to $75 in the old age pensions paid to widows and unmarried women at age 60. We are unable to find anything to that effect in the budget, in fact, we find exactly the opposite.
All that was very useful before the election. But afterwards, I bet that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) have never even thought of it. Those were only election promises, Mr. Speaker.
With respect to the budget properly, one can notice that the Minister of Finance is concerned about several important questions, the main one being unemployment. I shall come back to this later on.
One of his major concerns besides unemployment, Mr. Speaker, has to do with the excessive outflow of capital to foreign countries. The Minister of Finance mentions that our balance of payments deficit on current account has averaged $1.2 billion in the past six years. One notices also a little further that the Minister of Finance mentions that while unemployment is the major problem, we must not overlook other problems, the most serious being the continuing deficit in our balance of international payments, with the budgetary deficits of the federal government being next. The most serious problem then is the continuing deficit in our balance of international payments.
I have received yesterday, or the day before, another booklet in English only, also from the dominion bureau of statistics, entitled "National Accounts and Balance on Payments of Dividends". What is it about? It concerns our international trade for three months, that is the first quarter of 1963, which shows a 28902-5-89J
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire deficit of $243 million. For the exchange of goods there is a surplus of $62 million for a three-month period. On the other hand, there is a deficit in the matter of payments, capital transactions, of some $305 million in three months. This is due to dividends of $154 million and interest of $60 million and other short term capital transactions which form a total of $305 million.
So, when the Minister of Finance says that the most serious problem is still the balance of payments, the cause is inevitably the outflow of our capital by way of interest and dividends.
But what does the minister say then? Let us see what the Minister of Finance has to say on that subject.
There is a clearly recognized danger that if deficits continue at this rate, they will lead to a growing measure of control of our economy passing abroad.
In that respect, we certainly agree with the Minister of Finance; he is perfectly right.
But a little further he says;
In view of this situation we are entitled to take pride in the harmonious relations which have been maintained with the holders of foreign capital in Canada.
Mr. Speaker there is certainly a mistake there, either in the translation or the drafting, because the Minister of Finance warns us against too large a control by foreign capital and, the next moment, that is a few pages later, he tells us that we can take pride in the harmonious relations which exist with the holders of foreign capital.
He did not say it only once but he repeated it about two pages further in his budget address. I quote:
Above all, I am convinced that a growing partnership between Canadians and investors abroad is the best way of strengthening the harmonious relations with foreign capital which it is our object to preserve.
There you have another inconsistency, Mr. Speaker. But there is no end to inconsistencies in the field. About 12 pages further, the Minister of Finance said:
I referred earlier this evening to the need for a continuing inflow of foreign capital.
And I repeat what he said:
-the need for a continuing flow of foreign capital.
And there you have yet another inconsistency.
A little further, Mr. Speaker, the minister said:
As I indicated earlier, it is the policy of this government to encourage direct foreign investment in new enterprises in this country.

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire
But in the very same paragraph-and this is when I began to think I had not been given a true copy of the budget address-* he added:
It is our view that non-resident take-overs of established Canadian companies rarely confer any benefit on the Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, those are the contradictions we find in the address of the Minister of Finance. On the other hand, I found in it a rather encouraging passage-at least I hope we shall feel encouraged before long. On page 2 of his address, the Minister of Finance, speaking about our very heavy international balance of payments deficit, said:
This has meant that we have been importing goods and services which we should have produced at home-
But what are the most important services which we have imported from abroad? Foreign capital of course.
However, we heard the minister state that we should have produced at home services which we have been importing.
Mr. Speaker, why does the Minister of Finance not use an institution which is at his command, I mean the Bank of Canada? Why does he not use the Bank of Canada to find at home the services, or in other words the funds which are required?
This is but one of the measures we suggest to the Minister of Finance. If he were willing to put it into practice, he might solve some of the current problems, more particularly the problem of our international balance of payments deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I am not too surprised that the budget should give the results we have seen today considering especially that the Minister of Finance has based his whole argument and the budget on the confidence that the government of the day has created in Canada. Listen to this carefully:
As I say, our country Is just recovering from the loss of confidence that was engendered by the poor financial and economic administration of the previous government.
The minister adds the following:
However, confidence is not an element on which you can rely or which can be measured physically. It is a state of mind, a psychological phenomenon.
I do not have to go any further since that gives us an idea of the financial policy the government advocates. We all know that the best music teachers are not always the best singers. The best professors of economics are not always the best economists.
[Mr. Gregoire.l
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the members for Outremont-St. Jean, Drummond-Arthabaska and Matapedia-Matane (Messrs. Lamontagne, Pepin and Tremblay) will agree with me when I say that political economy could be defined as the science which deals with the production, exchange and consumption of the natural and industrial resources of a country. Indeed, that is the very definition that my hon. friends learned and taught. Political economy is a science-that word is most important-which is based on statistics, facts and figures just like physics is based on accurate figures.
When a rocket is launched in the atmosphere it is with the help of facts and statistical data, not through a state of mind or thanks to a psychological phenomenon.
If American physicists were to administer their interplanetary program through a psychological state of mind, they would not get their rockets off the ground.
The economists of the Liberal government have never considered economics as a science. In their opinion, it is a state of mind, a psychological phenomenon. That is why we are not getting anywhere. We have not even started off. That is also why the Minister of Finance stated: We could have procured commodities and services at home but we went abroad to get them.
If we are in such a pitiful situation today, it is because the government fails to realize that economics is a science based on statistics and accurate data and that economists should analyse the latter and use the Bank of Canada to provide credit in accordance with the possibilities and resources of the country. It is also because our economists are only concerned with states of mind and psychological phenomena.
With one hand, we give $52 million to go and get $360 with the other. This a psychological phenomenon. We maintain the deficit budget as before; these again are psychological phenomena.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that our economists should go back to school and become scholars in economics and not people who believe in chance, chance of the seven fat cows and the seven lean cows. I have heard before the President of the Privy Council speaking about progression and regression cycles, just like the seven fat cows and the seven lean cows. At that time, he lived on a psychological phenomenon.

speechtext:
I must thank the hon. members for letting me continue my remarks.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the second serious problem, second only to the problem of international trade balance is the problem of the national debt. The budget speech mentions the debt, but it is mainly concerned with the interest aspect of it, namely $918 million, which caused the heavy deficit of this government.
I believe that this is a most important matter. It has been raised on several occasions previously, therefore I will certainly be permitted to come back to it and ask the Minister of Finance to consider-it is true that I do not represent a large financial group, I am only a member of this house- but I would suggest to him that he consider the proposal I made to him in connection
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire with refinancing the national debt through the Bank of Canada. This way, we could pay the nation's debt and at the same time the service charges in the amount of $918 million.
Mr. Speaker, I shall refrain from dealing with one or two problems and, since my time is running short, I shall come to a point the Minister of Finance raised in his budget speech, and I quote:
I shall begin with a word regarding monetary policy.
At that point, the Minister of Finance dealt with this government's monetary policy. You will see what great monetary policy we have.
This government favours the kind of credit conditions which will encourage economic expansion. In saying this I am aware, of course, that our balance of payment situation must at all times be kept in mind.
Then we come to the policy which, to sum up the three paragraphs dealing with monetary policy, mean simple weekly visits to the governor of the Bank of Canada.
A little further in the speech we find the following statement:
The royal commission on banking and finance will no doubt be considering whether-
In other words he repeated that he shall meet almost continually with the governor of the Bank of Canada. This is the only element I seem to be able to find in the present day monetary policy of this government.
There was another Minister of Finance, some 20 years ago, who had very advanced ideas on the nation's monetary policy. In 1942, the Minister of Finance in the Liberal administration of the day implemented an important monetary reform. He eliminated the small five cent coin to replace it with a large nickel.
Another point on which I would like to insist today is that again and again, during his budget speech, the Minister of Finance talked about the take-over of our economy and indicated that Canadians must take over the economy of the country. In fact, here is what he said on that matter and there again inconsistencies can be noted.
But we must recognize that the extent of nonresident ownership and control which it has produced in Canada goes far beyond anything found in other countries in a comparable stage of industrial maturity.
So, the minister recognizes that there is a problem in that respect. And he added immediately:
-we are entitled to take pride in the harmonious relations which have been maintained with the holders of foreign capital in Canada.

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire
And even if the minister recognizes that foreigners hold a very substantial ownership of our economy, he suggests provisions or at least makes observations with a view to encouraging foreigners to acquire a greater part of our economy.
And when the minister proposes to reduce the taxes in a proportion of 5 per cent for corporations, when 25 per cent of their shares are held by Canadians, he really thinks he will assist Canadian industry. For that matter,
I can foresee that Canada will no longer be a country in which 75 per cent of the industry is controlled in a proportion of 100 per cent by foreigners, but a country in which 100 per cent of the industry is controlled in a proportion of 75 per cent by foreign interests.
For the information of the minister, I must tell him that when you require only 25 per cent Canadian ownership, you want to leave nothing but crumbs to Canadians so that the greater proportion of 75 per cent is left to foreign interests because it is a known fact that the one who owns 51 per cent of the shares of a company is still the one who controls the company and not the one who owns only 25 per cent. On that occasion, the Minister of Finance gave us evidence that instead of being 100 per cent Canadian, the present government is only 25 per cent Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, I would have liked to say more about the new taxes, but since my allotted time forbids me to do so, I shall talk about the federal-provincial fiscal relations.
In my opinion, the budget speech of the Minister of Finance has put an end to the hopes of those who believed that the relations between the central government and the government of the province of Quebec would be improved, thanks to a better distribution, and even through the return to the province of her sources of revenue.
In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance seemed to bring to an end the hopes of the government of the province of Quebec for the recovery of 25 per cent of personal and corporate income taxes. But when we consider that the objective of the province of Quebec is not only to recover 25 per cent but indeed 100 per cent of her sources of revenue, we may rest assured that from now on we shall have to fight a battle which will result in the victory for the ideas *of the province of Quebec in this field, despite the ideas put forward by the Minister *of Finance.
The Minister of Finance stated that the government would be able to have more influence on the economic activity through fiscal policy; I must tell him that he is completely

wrong, because we cannot influence the economy by keeping all fiscal policies. On the contrary, we impose restriction on the economy of a country, because taxes increase steadily instead of decreasing, and as taxes increase steadily, they always result in restrictions. Now, if the government reduced taxes in a substantial way, then we might say that a certain amount of influence could be felt, but in our country, taxes have always increased and never decreased.
Mr. Speaker, before resuming my seat, may I say that the present budget is stagnant and shows that the government is lacking in imagination, in daring, in energy and in vigour. Indeed, I suggest that the government should be more confident in the future of Canada, in the Canadian people and in the capacity for development of our country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I began preparation of this speech some time ago and today I find myself somewhat inhibited as to the remarks I had proposed to make on this occasion. Possibly it is a sign of old age, a certain mellowing of my disposition, but I have a certain reluctance about kicking somebody who is already down, and when one sees the government which came into office with such a fanfare of trumpets a few months ago in such complete disarray today, it is a saddening sight.
There are, after all, elements of Greek tragedy about this and I cannot help thinking that the unfortunate Minister of Finance is a victim of what the old Greeks called the sin of hubris, overweening pride, which invites the furies, of course, and the inevitable punishment. I am not competent to go into the vexed question of the legality or illegality of the hon. gentleman's use of unorthodox aid, or advisers, in the preparation of his budget. In view of recent revelations, I am not quite sure whether we should regard this as anything very sinister but rather in the nature of an old-fashioned quilting bee in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) gathered around him an assemblage of people to help him patch together a patchwork quilt made out of a lot of scraps of pre-Keynesian economies, tattered attempts at modern economics, and in the end producing a bed cover that is not going to keep us very warm in the forthcoming cold weather. I do not think this is too sinister now in that regard, but I do say that this house has a right to ask the government to make sure that if it is going to get unorthodox help from outside, that that

help should be competent. Because unfortunately the events of the last two days have proved that the help the minister relied on was grossly incompetent and should never have been permitted near the budget-making, not for fear that they would reveal secrets but because they were hopelessly incompetent to perform the tasks that the minister expected of them. I have no particular tears to shed over those in our society who failed to make a fortune yesterday, and I hold no brief for those who did. But I do suggest that if the minister is going to conduct our economic affairs on the basis of some sort of equity, then we should allow all thieves to have a licence at the same time.
In the course of his long address the minister mentioned on a number of occasions that to him the overriding problem in Canada today was that of unemployment, and with that estimate I am sure very few of us would disagree. He also said something else in the course of his long address on the budget, and when I read it today I wondered if this was the sentence that the furies were listening to. You recall, Mr. Speaker, that he told us that there has been a resurgence of confidence since the election. We would all agree with him that unemployment is the major problem of today, but I would suggest that it is possible to overestimate the power of words, and that unless they are translated into action and into reality they tend to become blown away by the winds of time. Our finance minister made a bow, I may say a much less pronounced bow than he made in his volume which dealt with a former troubled Canada, presumably a different one from the Canada that is troubled today, a very slight bow in the direction of acknowledging the role that deficit financing has in periods of economic stagnation and high unemployment. I was relieved to hear him say that, but then astounded a few minutes later to hear him produce a complete non sequitur and to proceed to chase a "will o' the wisp" of a balanced budget when he told us that we must begin now to move towards balancing the budget under conditions of high employment. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the 500,000 or however many unemployed there are today will be completely stupefied by this statement of the minister and will be asking themselves, what high employment is the man taking about? This move in the direction of a balanced budget is, of course, well calculated by every respectable economic opinion in the country, and indeed in the world, to prove a complete
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron obstacle to attaining that period of high employment and economic activity towards which the minister is looking.
I looked up some of the minister's earlier statements before he was promoted to his present position. He was a private member of this house on October 22, 1962, and on that date, as reported at page 817 of Hansard, he had this to tell us:
Our kind of economy works best in circumstances where responsibility for economic decision making is decentralized and in so far as possible is kept in private hands. However, it has been necessary in the past to invest some public capital in large undertakings and developments when sufficient private capital was not available. I think we should be perfectly willing to do the same thing again when it is necessary to get industrial developments going.
I am interested in that statement when I compare it with what the minister has been telling us in the last few days in his budget address. I wonder if he has decided that our economy was not in such a perilous condition as he was telling us eight months ago, and that he was mistaken; or can he possibly be telling us that in the course of these magic 60 days this government has solved all these problems and that they are now no longer with us? Because obviously if large capital expenditures of public funds were necessary eight months ago, one would assume that they were necessary today. But the minister seems to have changed his mind.
Admittedly the government came into power with stars in their eyes, and even though those stars have become a little tarnished in recent days no doubt there is enough glitter in them yet to blind them to some facts in this fact-finding budget. Fact number one, and it is one of which I would have thought the Minister of Finance would be aware, is that you do not cure depressed economic conditions by a hold-the-line policy. Yet that is what he outlined in his budget address. This was to be a hold-the-line policy, and he took great pride in the fact that he was going to reduce by some $200 million the deficit that had been anticipated by his predecessor in office.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this strikes me as rather peculiar when we compare the situation with things which happen in other parts of the world. For instance, in Sweden, which is a country of high economic activity at the present time, they have been prepared to maintain over a very long period of time, and are maintaining it to the present day in conditions of almost complete full employment, a deficit of somewhere in the neighbourhood of 2.9 per cent of their gross national product. Our Minister of Finance, in the face of unemployment and a stagnating economy,

The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron takes pride in the fact that he hopes to reduce this ratio between our deficit and our gross national product to some 1.5 per cent. I suggest to you that this indicates a complete lack of understanding of the role of modern economics in solving these problems. He has, of course, a number of measures in addition to the budget which he intends to use as incentives to economic stimulation. One of them is the old one which has been brought up year after year by both Conservative and Liberal governments-the idea that the way you get prosperity is to give tax incentives to private entrepreneurs. They persist in doing this even to the present day and even in the face of authoritative statements on the part of such organizations as the Canadian tax foundation, which reveal the real relationship between tax levels and levels of investment.
Between 1955 and 1957, as I am sure the Minister of Finance must know having come across this in the operations of his private business, there was a booming investment in Canada. At that time levels of corporation taxation ran from 45.9 per cent on profits over $500,000, 41.6 per cent on profits over $100,000, 36.2 per cent over $50,000, and so on. In 1962 the rate on profits of $500,000 and over was reduced to 39 per cent, on $100,000 and over to 30.9 per cent, and on $50,000 and over to 20.7 per cent. I suggest to you that this is clear proof that tax incentives are not what is required to stimulate private investments. What is required, of course, is effective demand.
This brings me to another of the items in this government's extraordinary incentive program. The Atlantic development board is going to be encouraged in its operations by providing a three-year tax holiday for firms which will enter that particular part of the country. In fact, it is being suggested to them that they will have a tax exemption for three years in which they could have no hope of making profits, because if there had been that hope they would have been there. The records show that if there were profits available, then firms would be there.
The minister has some rather curious method by which he plans to stimulate the economy. One of these has been discussed at intervals or attempts have been made to discuss it, and you have been hard put, Mr. Speaker, to head off a debate on it. I refer to the extension of the sales tax to building materials. This, in my opinion, is one of the most extraordinary combinations of measures ever presented by a Minister of Finance. We are told on the one hand that the government intends to stimulate building activity, particularly in the winter, by making a minis-
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
cule reduction in interest rate, by reducing the down payment and by providing a $500 bonus to those who undertake building in the winter. Then, in order to completely offset that the minister is going to extend the sales tax to all building material. Of course, the building of houses is only a part, perhaps a very small part, of the economy that is going to be battered by this expansion of the sales tax.
One can readily see what is going to happen when we read the report from the Ottawa city council last night. As a result of the minister's decision to extend the sales tax to building materials, they are going to sharply reduce their capital expenditures in the forthcoming year. This will be a great help to employment in the capital city. This action, of course, will be repeated in every city in Canada. It will find its reflection also in other major construction projects. We have, in my own province of British Columbia, some major construction projects which are in the wind, one at least of which it is contemplated will be undertaken. The added cost now provided by the minister's expansionary measure may stall proceedings on these projects.
What does he expect to get out of it? Here is the amazing part of it. The most he hopes to get out of it is $170 million. I am going to suggest he will not even get that because he will find that the quantities of materials on which the 11 per cent tax would be paid will sharply decline. In addition to that, the government's expenditures are going to go up as a result of coping with the consequent unemployment. Nothing could have been more spendthrift and irresponsible than this ridiculous method of pretending to stimulate the economy.
Then, we come to the municipal loans provision. I have mentioned the city council of Ottawa, and I should like to mention some comments in general terms about it. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is all inextricably mixed up with the budget. The loans to municipalities are going to exclude the very things that are the great problems of municipalities, the provision of such things as schools, hospitals, sewers and public housing. In fact, one is almost at a loss to know upon what a municipality is supposed to spend the money. Perhaps it could be used to raise aldermen's salaries or something of that sort. It is a very difficult thing to know what they could possibly do.
Then, we have the Canadian development corporation which is going to solve all our economic troubles by bringing some order into the investment field. However, this is not an expansionary measure at all. It is a measure that is only going to pool existing savings

unless the government is contemplating that it will have to make good on the various guarantees it is going to give. Otherwise, this will not be expansionary at all. This will merely be changing existing capital, existing savings, from one field to another.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister has-I will not say fallen from grace because he has not fallen yet-been under considerable fire over another of his measures to rectify the errors in the Canadian economy. I am very sympathetic to his idea that it is time Canada, the Canadian people and the Canadian government took a very long, serious look at this growing development of foreign ownership of our resources and our industry. But what an extraordinary way he went about trying to achieve that laudable purpose. I will not go again into the tizzy he caused in the stock market which set it bouncing around like a yo-yo. I am glad to find that some of the millionaires are in Vancouver. After all, it is time we had our share of the millionaires. However, this strikes me as typical of the methods by which this government, this Minister of Finance, proposed to solve the problem of foreign ownership.
They also have something which I think might be called the Liberal party's apostles creed. In the budget address we find a paragraph which starts with, "We believe":
We believe that industry in Canada, wherever it is controlled, should operate with due regard to the over-all interest of Canadians and the Canadian economy. This means that Canadian raw materials should be processed to the greatest possible extent in Canada ... It means that export markets should be sought actively wherever they may be found-
-a conscious effort to purchase its raw materials, components and supply from Canadian sources whenever those sources are competitive.
It means that industry should employ Canadian service firms wherever possible-
It means that industry should exert itself to expand in Canada all the industrial functions which can efficiently be carried on here-
It means that industry should seek to provide the fullest opportunity for Canadian employees at all levels, including managerial, scientific and technical personnel.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, our Minister of Finance would have our national economy organized on the basis of categorical imperatives. Unfortunately, the categorical imperative does not apply. No doubt these people should do this sort of thing, and no doubt they would have been doing it today had it been the profitable thing for them to do. Our finance minister does not suggest how we are going to persuade or convince them that this is the most profitable thing for them to do.
Then, of course, at the tail end of this curious group he has here, I was very interested to find this statement. It is rather ironic to read it today in the wake of yesterday's events:
The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron
Above all, I am convinced that a growing partnership between Canadians and investors abroad is the best way of strengthening the harmonious relations with foreign capital which it is our object to preserve. Foreign investors can further the growth of this partnership by selling minority interests in their enterprises to Canadians-
Again, this is something they should do, but there is no indication of just how we are going to get them to do this. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance, like all previous ministers of finance in Canada, in trying to deal with this problem is trying to deal with something that is insoluble within the framework of our traditional economic and social relationships For one thing, we have a constitutional problem in Canada to be considered because the provinces have complete control over the bulk of the natural resources on which foreign corporations have built their industries.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, there is only one sort of solution for this problem, the solution of public investment to regain control of the resources on which these industries are based, and if the federal government were to embark on a program of financial assistance to provinces prepared to embark on such a recovery of their natural resources I think this would be the sensible way to go about the problem of foreign ownership. Certainly none of the methods provided by the minister are anything but derisory in their nature.
We have also heard quite a bit in the budget debate about the question of liberalizing trade. Our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) has gone through the world, and he is hoping he did something at GATT that will help our problems. I should like to ask him and also ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) this. It is asked quite seriously and I hope they have given some consideration to it. About a month ago the Right Hon. Harold Wilson, speaking to the United States chamber of commerce in London, pointed out the dangers of merely liberalizing trade without taking some steps in regard to international liquidity. I have no doubt whatever that the Minister of Trade and Commerce noted this speech and the proposals that were made by Mr. Wilson at that time, proposals, incidentally, that have been made before by economists. Dr. Triffin was one, and in a much earlier time, of course, a similar proposal was made by the late John Maynard Keynes. The proposal was that the international monetary fund should be established in effect as an international central bank.
Mr. Wilson points out that in the world as a whole we are now facing exactly the same problem that national economies were facing at the time they were tied to gold and which required increases in the volumes

The Budget-Mr. C. Cameron of gold before there could be economic expansion. He points out that we are in virtually the same position today internationally and that sooner or later we have to take steps in that regard in establishing the international monetary fund or a similar international body as, in effect, an international central bank enabled to create credit for the development of the undeveloped areas, and also in order to enable developed countries to avoid the recurring exchange crises which the present situation always imposes upon them when expansionary policies are embarked upon. I should like to hear at some time from the government whether they have taken part in any such discussions, whether they have advanced any of these ideas at international gatherings and what their views on this matter are.
I have been criticizing the government's budget, but I do not think that is enough for a member of the house to do. I think we should also present our ideas of what sort of things the budget should have attempted to do and I have attempted in very rough terms to present some projects that we should be understaking in Canada, with their probable costs or possible costs, shall we say. For instance, I understand that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) has today announced an increase in the old age pension of $10. I would suggest on behalf of this party that this is not going nearly far enough, that there has gone on for long enough in Canada the pathetic picture of people who reach the age of 65, who are forced into retirement by their employers and have five years to wait before they can draw the old age pension. We claim that we shall not be dealing with this problem until we bring the 65 to 69 group under the old age pension at the rate of $75 a month. With the increase granted today there will be a total there of some $500 millions.
Then we have something that has been promised to the people of Canada year after year by successive Liberal governments, and more recently by a Conservative government, and that is a comprehensive national plan of health insurance. It is very difficult to estimate what the cost of such a plan would be. Some estimates run as high as $500 million and suggest that the federal government's share would be some $300 million.
Then we have the question of the municipal loan fund which the government is proposing. I suggest to you, sir, that $400 million spread over three years will have the most minute effect in stimulating the economy and that the amount should be something more in the order of $300 million or $400 million a year, once the municipalities get under way on this project. Then there is the question of the difference in the interest rate on these loans.
[Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands) .1
I do not think we have been told what that is to be. Certainly unless the government is going to shoulder quite a bit of the cost of the interest rate the municipalities are not going to be in a position to borrow from the fund, as the government apparently hopes they are going to do.
I suggest to you. Mr. Speaker, that these suggestions for very great increases of governmental expenditure, with their consequent deficits, are in no way out of line with the experience of countries which are at least as progressive as Canada and which are at least as economically efficient as Canada, and that we should be considering taking a leaf out of their books. I mentioned earlier and I repeat now that in Sweden there has been for many years a deficit carried by the government of anything up to 3 per cent of their gross national product and that today in a time of full employment in Sweden it is still 2.9 per cent of the Swedish gross national product; whereas the deficit so proudly announced by the minister, unless he is adding to it today or tomorrow-we do not know and we will never be sure-amounts to some 1.5 per cent of the gross national product. That in itself in my view condemns this government and this budget and, as I said on budget night, "presented as a means of stimulating the economy, it is nothing but a fraud".
I would beg the government and hon. members in all parties not to be frightened by the sort of suggestions I have made, with their large deficits perhaps running up into billion and a half figures, because these are the sort of figures that progressive countries are now adopting. I would remind you, sir, that without blinking an eye we are prepared to spend very much more than that on defences which so far have proved rather dubious.
These things will not, of course, solve our problems permanently. We in this group do not think they can be solved permanently within the terms of our present economy but they will give it a breathing spell in order to lay the groundwork for those sweeping social and economic changes which are obviously on the horizon. With the ever more collective world of which the eloquent and charming lady member for Northumberland spoke in the first speech to this twenty sixth parliament-

Finally, Mr. Speaker, let me say that as a Canadian, as one who has lived nearly all his life in Canada, as one whose children and grandchildren have been born here, it affords me no pleasure to see the government of my country in such hopeless disarray as it is today. I would conclude as my final word to the government on this occasion: For heaven's sake, pull yourselves together. We cannot afford any more of these follies, any more of these ineptitudes, because all the rest of we Canadians have to cringe along with you at the ridiculous spectacle you are presenting to the rest of the world.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONES
PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-ll, to amend the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act (twelve mile fishing zone).
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to extend the present three mile fishing limit to 12 miles off our shores. It would also provide a year for negotiations to that end. I hope for its passage today, or at least for its referral to committee where it might be discussed in line with other pending legislation of a similar nature.
I am very well aware of the fact that the government has announced its intention of introducing legislation to establish the 12-mile limit, and I have earlier congratulated the government on that intention. However, I have left my bill on the order paper because I am not yet just sure what kind of 12-mile limit the government has in mind, and I am not sure whether the government knows exactly itself. It may be, that, as in some other departments, there are changes to be made, or that the policy is not quite clear on that point.
Another reason for leaving the bill on the order paper is because I think it affords a timely example of how the passage of time enables the administration to catch up with the policies of the party I represent, because this bill was introduced last session and also in the session of 1961. In both sessions it either failed to reach second reading or was talked out. However, it is still here today, and the bill states clearly what it means. It represents the views of the great bulk of the fishing industry, particularly in the Pacific area with which I am most familiar, and it would give those rights to Canadian fishermen which fishermen in so many other countries enjoy.

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act
It calls for:
-a declaration by the Queen in parliament that Canada within those twelve marine miles seaward of her coasts has, to the sole use and benefit of her nationals, the right to fish exclusive of all others: as well as an affirmation of Canada's obligation to protect and conserve the live resources of those seas to that same end.
The bill would repeal section 2(b) of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act and substitute the following therefor:
(b) 'Canadian territorial waters' means a fishing zone extending seaward to a limit twelve nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of the territorial seas of Canada are measured headland to headland and includes inland waters of Canada.
The bill is in geographical line with the stand taken by the Fisheries Council of Canada and such organizations as the united fishermen and allied workers' union of B.C. It represents the feeling of the great bulk of the fishing industry on both coasts.
The fisheries council, for instance, presses for the 12 mile limit and also proposes the straight headland to headland baseline which would enclose national waters. In the Pacific this baseline would go from headland to headland along the west side of Vancouver island and the Queen Charlotte islands, and the 12-mile exclusive area would extend seaward from that line. In the Atlantic it would connect at the international boundary and enclose the bay of Fundy and gulf of St. Lawrence.
It may be worthy of note that a special committee of the B.C. legislature has endorsed the 12-mile limit, and has urged also that Canada take unilateral action, if necessary, to establish the baseline and declare exclusive fishing rights for a distance of 12 miles from this baseline, and "be prepared to enforce such measures".
In other parts of the world the 12-mile limit for territorial waters has been established by Iceland, Norway and Russia since the 1960 Geenva conference. Denmark has set the 12-mile limit around Greenland, and Iceland has successfully established her 12-mile zone even against active opposition. I think, Mr. Speaker, that Canada, like so many other countries, should now take the perfectly reasonable step of staking out her 12-mile limit and offering time to others to negotiate to that end. Over 50 countries have now established their fishing limits and one country, Peru, has actually established a fishing zone of 200 miles exclusive to itself.
However, I think that with respect to allowing the United States to continue to fish inside the 12-mile limit in the Pacific we had better understand at once that it is almost solely the United States who fishes there now. There will be little change in the betterment of our


Canadian fisheries industry if there is to be no change in who fishes in that zone. We look to the government, if it proceeds with the 12-mile legislation or brings forward other similar proposals, to do so upon the basis of putting Canada's interests first. We have no desire to injure our United States friends or their fishing interests, but we believe it is a reasonable proposition that Canada should establish her own rights and limits and be willing to negotiate to keep them. We can undertake to respect the 12-mile fishing limits of other lands on the basis of their respecting ours.
Mr. Speaker, Canada needs to have the reasonable protection this bill can provide. On the east coast the large Canadian trawlers are by law kept 12-miles out so as not to destroy the inshore nursery grounds with their heavy trawls. Big trawlers of numerous nations, however, fish right up to our three-mile limit and on occasion have had the gall to call up the Canadian patrol boats upon seeing Canadian trawlers fishing closer than 12 miles and have asked that they be arrested. The bill before us also follows along the line of the former administration's ideas as expressed in the proposal of the Canadian government at the end of 1959 by the then secretary of state for external affairs at the United Nations conference on the law of the sea. We agreed with the position taken by the government at that time, but we did not agree with their failure or inability to bring about the establishment of this 12-mile zone. The present government, as I understand it from what has been announced, has decided upon the establishment and adoption of the principle of the 12-mile limit and has probably worked out some details for putting this decision into legislative form. So that in the view of those in this party, the former administration and the present government we have a very large measure of agreement in the house on the need for such legislation. I think this agreement is shared particularly by all hon. members from British Columbia, no matter to what party they belong.
I think we should realize, however, that the mere establishment of this zone will not solve our fisheries problems. British Columbia salmon, for instance, are caught as far as
1,000	miles from shore; sometimes they are found 2,000 miles out from their home in the Fraser river area. The 12-mile limit will assist in conservation but it will do little to improve Canadian salmon harvesting. But bottom fish will be protected by the 12-mile zone, and this will certainly be a benefit to Canada.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I personally am very much impressed by the views of Senator Reid who comes from my own constituency

of New Westminster. He is an authority of many years and has a great deal of knowledge on this question. He has stated that in the protection of our fisheries Canada cannot ignore Russia. Russia has large and efficient floating cannery fleets heading down the Pacific coast which are much more modern than our own fishing units. They are not doing anything illegal but they interfere with our nets. This is a problem for us because of the present lack of efficient or effective regulations to control them. This also applies to Japan. If the United States, Japan and Canada are to come to some agreement regarding their share of the conservation and harvesting of the Pacific fisheries they must, in my opinion, bring Russia into such an agreement and make her subject to the over-all Pacific fishery regulations. Our fisheries could be put in a very grave situation, whether or not we establish a 12-mile limit, if Japan drops out of the Pacific agreement, because she may well ask why she should hold her hand while Russia does not.
The situation in the Pacific is that of a pool of water in which four people are fishing, three of them under some form of co-operative agreement and the fourth is not. This produces an embarrassing situation and makes it most difficult to proceed with any advantage, whether or not we obtain a 12-mile fishing limit, although this would certainly remove some part of the problem.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put on the record, so we may get a proper perspective of the matter, the fishing catches of the major Pacific fishing nations for 1961. These figures are in metric tons, which are 240 pounds more than our own. We find, for example, that in 1961 Japan caught 6,711,000 tons; the U.S.S.R.,	3,250,000; the United
States, 2,874,000; and Canada, 1,000,400. I would urge all hon. members to support this measure, which I think is timely. If it should not be approved, I would hope that at least it might be referred to the appropriate committee for further detailed consideration.

If hon. members look at section 2(b) of the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act they will see envisaged in that section two methods by which Canada can acquire territorial waters. One is by designation by act of parliament or the governor in council, and the other is in any event those waters contained within three miles of our coasts. The amendment the hon. member proposes strikes out one of those methods that by which we can acquire territorial jurisdiction by act of parliament or declaration of the governor in council. This is a rather small point, but I think it is a very important one. Either now or in the future Canada's sovereignty in certain sections of our far north may be called into question, and I think it should be very clear in our statutes that we are entitled by act of parliament to declare sovereignty and jurisdiction over those areas. No doubt that is something which can be cleared up in committee.
The hon. member for New Westminster made reference to some of the aspects of the fishing industry in British Columbia. I should like to add to those remarks in order that hon. members who are not from the west coast may realize the tremendous importance which the fishing industry is to us. The industry employs some 14,000 independent fishermen. In 1961, the department, as will be shown in its annual report, issued 21,898 commercial fishing licences. About
6.000	plant and packing boat workers are directly dependant on the industry and some
75.000	are indirectly dependant upon it. Production on a five-year average totals some $71.5 million worth of fish, fish products, oil and meal, 60 per cent of which is exported, a most important consideration to the economy of our country.
Our fishing industry operates up and down the whole coast, from the United States border in the south to the Alaska Panhandle and the Bering sea in the north. Many areas in British Columbia are entirely dependant on the fishery. This is particularly true of our Indian population which is scattered up and down the coast in isolated bays and inlets in small communities on reserves. Their well-being is totally dependant on the fish they catch. The cultivation and maintenance of our fishery resources is vitally important to the province, not only because of the economic advantages the industry brings to the country but also because thousands of our

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act fishermen, their wives and their children, are looking to the resources of the sea for their future livelihood.
The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned that there are several ways of protecting our resources. I am sure many in this chamber are familiar with them. All the work of the Department of Fisheries is connected with the protection of our resources. The establishment of artificial spawning beds, catch limits, restrictions on gear and so on are ways in which this protection is afforded, but the two most important means of protection were those mentioned by the hon. member, namely, the means provided in this act and by the government in its declaration with regard to the establishment of a 12-mile limit to protect our coastal and inshore fisheries, and membership in international agreements to protect our resources on the high seas.
It is important to point out that the provision of a 12-mile limit is not a complete answer to the protection of our resources. Canada in the past has always shown a great willingness to co-operate with other nations in the protection of her resources on the high seas. At the present time we are members of some seven international agreements relative to fishing and the resources of the seas. These are the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which deals with sockeye and chum salmon on the Fraser; the international Pacific halibut commission; the international north Pacific fisheries commission; the international commission for the northern Atlantic fisheries; the great lakes fisheries commission; the north Pacific fur seal commission, and the international whaling commission.
It is essential that we should protect our fishery resources by maintaining our membership in these international agreements. This is the only way in which we can protect our resources on the high seas. I say this particularly because there are elements in British Columbia, some of which I think I can properly call irresponsible, which are now pouring scorn on the fact that Canada is a member of some of these agreements and issuing propaganda to the effect that we should pull out of them. If we are to protect our own interests on the high seas we must take all possible steps not only to preserve but to strengthen the terms of these agreements because, without them, foreign fleets could fish right up to our territorial limits.

I was referring to material which I have received advocating a policy which would, I think, destroy the north Pacific salmon agreement. Certain organizations are advocating a policy which, if adopted by the government, would in my opinion result in the members forsaking this agreement and leaving us without any agreement at all. The importance of this agreement to the west coast fisheries cannot be overemphasized.
As the hon. member for New Westminster said, the salmon is the truly important fish on the west coast. This is a fish which spawns in the rivers, goes down the river as a finger-ling and makes its way thousands of miles into the mid-Pacific to grow to full size before returning to the river of its birth. Under the NORPAC agreement our salmon are protected as they go out into the Pacific. To illustrate the importance to British Columbia of maintaining this agreement, I should like to quote briefly from the concluding observations of the fisheries association of British Columbia to the special committee on fisheries of the British Columbia legislative assembly:
The one salient fact that cannot be ignored, regardless of all emotional appeal designed to arouse a pseudo-nationalistic bravado, is that the north Pacific treaty and the abstention principle is all that is preventing the Japanese from exploiting the fishery resource of British Columbia within three miles of our shores.
To turn now to the bill itself and what it will mean for Canada, may I say that it involves two things. It involves the establishment of a baseline drawn from headland to headland. This means that the line from which we draw the 12-mile limit will not run parallel to the coastline but from one principal head land to the next. This, on the west coast, will mean the inclusion of such huge bodies of water as Queen Charlotte sound, Hecate straits and Dixon entrance.
On the east coast it will include the bay of Fundy and the gulf of St. Lawrence which will be of great benefit in protecting the eastern fisheries. Thus, when we talk of a 12-mile limit, it is important to remember that it is the intention of the government as stated in its declaration on June 4 to establish a territorial limit, to be drawn from headland to headland, for which there are

important precedents, as the hon. member pointed out. There are many nations which have already established their limits according to that principle, following the Anglo-Swedish case in 1951.
There are two ways of declaring a 12-mile limit. It is possible to declare such a limit for all purposes, or a government can establish what is called a divided territorial jurisdiction. Under such a system the limit would, for example, be divided into two distances of six miles each, or it could be divided in a different proportion. The first six miles, say, would be territorial waters for all purposes including defence, pollution, the enforcement of customs regulations, and so on. The additional six miles would be an exclusive fishing zone.
The bill before us provides for a 12-mile fishing or territorial limit for all purposes. I support the six by six formula by which we would draw our baseline from headland to headland, and from that baseline have a territorial jurisdiction for the first six miles and a fishing zone for the next six miles, giving a total fishing zone of 12 miles. The reason I suggest that the six by six formula would be better is because that was the formula involved in a resolution supported by Canada and the United States at the international conference on the law of the sea which received almost enough, but not quite enough, support to carry. It was sponsored jointly at the second United Nations conference on the law of the sea in 1960 by the United States and Canada. I should like to read the first two paragraphs of the resolution which we sponsored:
1.	A state is entitled to fix the breadth of its territorial sea up to a maximum of six nautical miles measured from the applicable baseline.
2.	A state is entitled to establish a fishing zone contiguous to its territorial sea extending to a maximum limit of twelve nautical miles from the baseline from which the breadth of its territorial sea is measured, in which it shall have the same rights in respect to fishing and the exploitations of the living resources of the sea as it has in its territorial sea.
I would support a six by six formula of territorial jurisdiction because it has been widely supported at this international conference. If we adopt that method of measurement those nations, including the United States, which supported our resolution at the international conference are going to have a far more difficult time now opposing Canada's declaration of this 12-mile limit. If they supported us at the international conference I suggest they can hardly oppose us now and say we are not entitled to make this declaration.
