subtopic: PROVISION FOR EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter under consideration is one of great interest to my province, and as a matter of fact to all the east coast area. It is a matter on which I have spoken in support on previous occasions. The proposal in the bill to extend fishing limits to 12 miles is one in which, as has been said already, there is a great deal of agreement. Such a proposal is long overdue, because if my reading of history is correct the problem of other nations utilizing our waters began almost as soon as Canada was discovered. In 1497 John Cabot discovered Newfoundland and Canada, and at the same time discovered that the waters of the area were full of fish. He began the real industrial

Coastal Fisheries Protection Act development of this nation. According to history, two years afterwards not only were the English fishing the area but the Basques, the Portuguese, and others, many of whom have fished there ever since. The problems which were created around the year 1500 have accumulated and multiplied, until it now becomes important to us to decide what we really mean when we say that Canada extends from sea to sea, whether our jurisdiction stops at the sea shore, or does in fact include Canadian territorial waters.
I agree with the sponsor of the bill that we must put Canada's interests first, and in doing that we are only doing our duty. We are not unmindful of the rights of others, but we must be mindful of the fact that the waters of Canada and what they produce are just as much Canadian as the soil of Canada and what it produces. It is unthinkable that the land of Canada should be exploited to the advantage of our competitors and those who are not Canadians. Is it not just as logical for us to assume that the waters of Canada and the fish contained therein belong to Canadians first, and that they should be looked upon as a great Canadian resource? We have not only to recognize this ourselves but to convince others as well.
The 12-mile limit in itself is not a cure-all. But it is a great help, and if it is applied on the baseline principle it will do two things. It will reserve for Canadians sections of waters to fish. At the same time it will contribute substantially toward conservation. Unfortunately that is not an answer in itself. If the 12-mile limit simply followed the contour of the coast and somewhat widened that thin fringe around our coast it would not be effective. If the baseline principle is observed and the line is drawn from headland to headland, waters within 12 miles from the coast would be considered Canadian and would become Canadian. We will have preserved for our fishermen that which is essential, if the fisheries of Canada are to be exploited as they ought to be, if the fishing industry is going to give the fishermen the living it ought to give them and if the productivity of the sea is going to give to Canada the income it ought to give. All these things will be accomplished by the institution of a 12-mile limit which is founded on the baseline principle.
Perhaps nothing is more evident than the fact that our waters are being exploited. Everybody knows it. The three-mile limit gives too narrow a fringe around the coast. It can easily be infringed upon over night, and often it is. It is a known fact that during the night ships do move inside the three-mile limit. Such a narrow strip of water is very difficult to police. Despite the fact that the

declaration of the 12-mile limit will mean there will be greater areas to police, it will be easier to protect this greater area of water than it is to protect the three-mile limit.
Figures show that Canada's production of fish is poor, and that in comparison the production of fish by other nations is rather alarming. We began the fishing industry in the western hemisphere. We have the wealthiest fishing ground in the world. We have allowed our competitors to take the fish away from us, and what is worse they have taken it away from within sight of our shores. These Canadian waters should be preserved for the use of Canadian fishermen. In my personal opinion the gulf of St. Lawrence ought to be a Canadian sea. I believe the same statement applies to the inland seas formed by the islands of the west coast. These, I believe, are vital to the survival of Canada as a great fishing country. These I believe to be vital, if our fishermen are going to have the use of the productive grounds much longer, because at the present time fish are being taken from within sight of our shores at such a rate that our fishermen will not have a chance to survive.
If our oldest industry goes it will adversely affect many thousands of people directly and indirectly, and will affect all of Canada. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I have often thought that because our fishing industry is so old it has, like a lot of old industries, accumulated the problems of centuries. We have been inclined not to look upon it in the light in which it ought to be viewed. Although the fishing industry is old, the production of the fishing industry is being used in ever greater amounts every year. Despite the fact that, like other ancient industries, it does have problems that have grown over the years, none of these problems is insurmountable. There is nothing wrong with the fishing industry which cannot be solved. The biggest problem facing the fishing industry is the fact that we look upon these problems as insoluble. However, in reality, we are faced with a group of small problems which, if attacked individually could be solved and the industry could be made much more profitable.
Figures prove, I believe, that there is more salt codfish being consumed today than there was 30 years ago. Salt codfish production is the oldest part of the industry. The fresh fish industry has been expanding rapidly. The problem is not that the world is using too little, although that might well be the case, of the products of the sea, but that we in Canada have not been getting our share of the world market. This is one problem that has to be tackled and it can be tackled

effectively, just as any other problem that affects the fishing industry can be attacked separately and solved.
Keeping in mind the existence of other problems, this is one that is basic, the establishment of a 12-mile limit founded on the baseline principle. This is necessary if we are going to reserve for Canadian use the sections of water along our coast which are highly productive of fish, waters which can be utilized by our fishermen in order that they may enjoy a better livelihood and make Canada's place in the world markets more secure than it is today.

The first is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has already announced that the government is going to proclaim this 12-mile limit. I believe that the principle is very sound and, furthermore, I believe that its necessity has been established without any question. The need has been indicated from two particular points of view: one, the saving of this particular resource for Canadian fishermen and, of course, the Canadian consumer as well; second, the principle of conservation and that representations have been made to the various parties in this house by those associated with the fishing industry. I do not believe anyone would question the importance of these two principles.
Not only have we had the presentation of this bill this afternoon, but we are reminded, of course, of the many other representations that have been made in connection with the establishment of the 12-mile limit. We have, for instance, the presentation that was made by a delegation from the united fishermen and allied workers' union during the last parliament. It was also reinforced by a delegation that was heard just recently and met, I believe, representatives of the various parties in the house. I should like to take one short paragraph from a publication that was issued by the united fishermen and allied workers' union headed, "Urgent appeal for action." Under the heading, "British Columbia fishermen strongly urge decisive action". I find this in paragraph number 4:
Declaration of a 12-mile territorial waters limit by the Canadian government. Our waters would
Coastal Fisheries Protection Act extend 12 miles outside of a "headland to headland" baseline drawn in such manner as to include the waters of Queen Charlotte sound, Hecate strait and Dixon entrance.
We also have a reference to this matter in a communication to the minister of fisheries under the former government from the amalgamated conservation society, which is made up of 12 associations and organizations. Paragraph 3 of their letter states:
The law of the sea conference held at Geneva in 1960 found Canada's proposed 12-mile limit defeated by only one vote. An acceptable agreement for a 12-mile limit had been worked out beforehand between the United States and Canada, why did these two nations not ratify an agreement on the 12-mile limit between themselves? Smaller nations in order to conserve their fisheries were forced to establish such a limit which they have enforced and for which they are to be commended.
Reference has also been made today to the report submitted by the special committee appointed by the British Columbia legislature to inquire into certain matters affecting the commercial fishing industry in British Columbia. I should like to read a paragraph from this report presented on March 26, 1963.
Your committee also noted basic agreement by all segments of the industry with the pressing need to amend the now obsolete three-mile limitation of Canada's territorial waters. All submissions advocated a straight baseline drawn from headland to headland of British Columbia's outer coastline, and to provide protection for Canadian fisheries for a distance of 12 miles to seaward in support of the arguments offered. As a result thereof your committee further recommends that another resolution containing this request be forwarded to the government of Canada, as follows:
Whereas precedent exists whereby nations have established the width of their territorial seas; and
Whereas the present 3-mile limit is inadequate for the protection of Canadian fisheries;
Therefore be it resolved, that Canada take unilateral action to establish a headland to headland baseline along its outer coastal shoreline as recommended jointly by Canada and the United States of America at the 1960 United Nations conference on the law of the sea; and
Be it further resolved, that Canada, while recognizing reciprocal fishing rights with the United States of America, declare exclusive fishing rights for a distance of 12 miles to seaward of that baseline; and
Be it further resolved, that upon such declaration, Canada be prepared to enforce such measures.
I think that these statements from the various organizations and from the British Columbia legislature point up the necessity of action on the particular bill that has been presented by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather). There is reference, of course, to historic rights, but I would suggest that we cannot allow our Canadian resources to be depleted or destroyed, nor can we deprive Canadian fishermen of their rightful first claim to those resources. As has been pointed out, and I mentioned this previously, from the two points of view of conserving our resources

We appreciated the reference in the speech from the throne to the effect that a fisheries program for Canada was going to be worked out in co-operation with the provinces. I do not know just how far this is going to go, but perhaps it will have some effect and influence on this particular matter.

I left my office before six o'clock last night and I was fully familiar with the budget, Mr. Speaker.
Then the leader of the New Democratic party said:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister if persons other than the officials of his department participated in the preparation of last night's budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker; various officials of various departments participated-*
But he did not say at that time that three consultants were brought in, outside of government officials. Then there was a question by the hon. member for Pontiac-Temisca-mingue (Mr. Martineau). I do not know if I would have put the question at that time because it was such that if he had got the opposite answer it would not have been such a good answer, because it was such a direct question; but I admire the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue who put the question to the minister and finally put his finger on the problem we are now debating:
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if any of the outside persons who advised him on budget matters were informed in advance of any of the contents of the budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think I can say any more.
He wanted to remain silent, but he did not remain silent too long because he knew then there was a storm brewing, not only in the House of Commons and across the country, but in the ranks who form the front of his party. Then the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) said to the Minister of Finance, "I think under the circumstances, with this type of interrogation, you must make a clean breast of the situation".

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that mind reading?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Crystal gazing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know whether it is mind reading or even crystal gazing that the Secretary of State often practises. I would ask these questions, and these are the questions we wanted answered at that time. Who were these people? What are their connections? What special interests do they represent? Like other previous speakers in reference to this matter, I want to make it quite clear that nothing I say in this regard


means that I am at this time, from the facts that are before us, suggesting that any of these men are not men of integrity, nor am I making any reflection on the integrity of the Minister of Finance. But facts are facts and the Canadian people are entitled to know how and in what manner this partisan document known as the budget is put together. Who were these people? What firms were they connected with? There was Dr. M. P. O'Connell, of Harris and Partners in Toronto, chartered accountants; there was Mr. G. A. Conway, a chartered accountant from Toronto, and Mr. D. C. H. Stanley of Wood, Gundy and Company. Two of these people are agents, employees, connected with, or owners or shareholders of the companies in question. These are two large financial institutions in the city of Toronto. After further interrogation it was suggested that these men had taken an oath of secrecy. Then there was a question as to whether or not there was an order in council. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said he had checked and there was no order in council. Then we had the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) saying, "Oh, well, it was not an order in council after all. We used a special act. They were actually hired by contract", like you buy and sell property. These are some of the things we want to find out. I suggest, first of all, that we should have a select committee composed of hon. members of this House of Commons. All the people connected with this matter should be brought before that committee, under oath, to give evidence. In this way we could determine the facts and this house would be in a position to come to a decision and pass judgment.
I ask this question: What precedent exists in reference to conduct such as having outsiders prepare the budget, such as having ghost writers prepare the budget? At first one was prone to ask: What is wrong with getting outside help? In fact, some of the newspapers asked this question. It was also asked: What is wrong with getting the most experienced brains to assist in the preparation of the budget? I think the Minister of Finance asked that himself. On the face of it there would appear to be nothing wrong; but what does precedent say about this, and what is the principle behind this precedent? The answer is clear in this regard, for it is based on a very sound principle and tradition, which is that the contents of our budget must be kept secret. Any violation of this principle, any indiscretion which might affect and undermine the principle of secrecy has in Great Britain, as well as in other countries which have the same parliamentary

system as our own, brought about the immediate resignation of the minister of finance who might have been guilty of such indiscretion. The principle is a very simple one. It is to avoid evil and the appearance of evil. I would point out also, as some other hon. members have done, that it is the standard procedure in Canadian parliamentary life that no persons other than members of the government and officials of the government shall have any knowledge of what is in the budget.
It must be remembered that these consultants were employed and attached to certain financial institutions which stood to make millions of dollars if they had prior knowledge of what was in the budget, and probably stood to lose millions of dollars if they did not have that knowledge. No one is suggesting-I repeat this-that these outsiders brought in as ghost writers actually informed their employers of the new tax structure as far as its affecting the sale of stocks and bonds was concerned. But to ask these people, these human beings, to carry this kind of load and not to use the information that they have now, and had at the time, when they are transacting business deals, is asking too much of any Canadian or any other person. I say that only supernatural men could be expected to toe the line in that regard, and I do not think anyone would suggest that these men are supernatural. I put this forward as an illustration of my point.
Anyone who has practised law before the bar of justice knows that sometimes in a most serious criminal case, such as murder, inadmissible evidence gets before the jury. The jury hear it and the judge hears it. The judge may advise the jury to overlook what they have heard, but we who are defending these people before the bar of justice profess that it is very difficult to clear one's mind of what one has heard. The jury may draw inferences from the facts, or what they think are inferences, because they had that knowledge deep-seated in their own minds.
There are two interesting precedents as far as secrecy of the budget is concerned. One concerns a cabinet minister in England by the name of the Hon. Mr. Thomas, who was the colonial secretary in 1936. What did he do? He merely remarked something about the price of some commodity, tobacco or tea-

speechtext: Beer.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it was beer. That may be a better commodity. He made some small remark as to the price of this commodity to a Mr. Butt, who was also a member of parliament. Mr. Butt then made some remark to someone else, and there was a leak of the budget contents. What happened? Mr. Thomas
The Budget-Mr. Woolliams resigned in 1936. I repeat, he was the colonial secretary and he resigned because of that indiscretion. I might mention there are some authorities in this connection. There is Keith's book on the British cabinet system, which says that the most fundamental thing in the preparation of the budget is secrecy, to avoid evil and the appearance of evil. I should like to quote from page 89 of this book, Mr. Speaker. It was said by the writer, who was dealing with this question, that even the closest cabinet colleagues should not have absolute knowledge of what is actually in the final draft of the budget; that only the minister of finance should have this knowledge, and the officials of the minister of finance in the government. Then he said this:
There are clear disadvantages in this procedure-
The Minister of Finance admits that; he said there were some disadvantages in not getting outside help, because apparently he did not feel he had the kind of officials who could do the job:
*-necessary though it may be in the interest of secrecy in so far as the chancellor is allowed to prepare his plans without the valuable aid which is naturally provided by examination by a committee of the cabinet.
In effect, Mr. Speaker, what Keith said in his book was that although, as was pointed out by the present Minister of Finance, there may be some disadvantage in not getting outside help or even help from a special committee of government officials, that disadvantage is overshadowed by the necessity that the facts in connection with the budget must at all times be kept secret, because otherwise individuals stand to enrich themselves, or could enrich themselves at the expense of their fellow men in society. Putting it in more simple terms, why should-and this is what Canadians across the country are asking tonight-three or four Canadians have this information prior to the budget coming down, when 18 million or 20 million Canadians must stand the rap of extra taxation when the budget is brought down? There is the fundamental principle behind the doctrine of secrecy that prevails when the budget is drafted. What happened? Mr. Thomas resigned. I do not know what ramifications may follow in reference to the present Minister of Finance. That is a responsibility he must assume himself and make his own decision on.
Let us for a few moments look at a second illustration. The second interesting resignation to which I refer is in reference to Sir Hugh Dalton. This is discussed fully in his memoirs which are called "High tide and after". These are his memoirs for the period 1945 to 1960. There is a chapter called "My resignation". What did he do? When he left his office

The Budget-Mr, Woolliams on the night he was going to deliver his budget he spoke to a fellow by the name of John Carvel, who was a correspondent for the Star, who was standing in the lobby.
He made a little remark to him in that regard. It was only some passing remark. Then he went to his place to deliver the budget. The next morning, when the cabinet ministers were attending a cabinet meeting, he got a note saying there had been some leakage of the contents of the budget. Immediately, he said he recalled making that statement and although there had been no harm done to the state, because very few newspapers had reached the public before the budget speech was delivered, he felt it was his duty to resign. And he did resign. These are his exact words used in the House of Commons. He said on that occasion in 1947:
I very much regret to tell the house that the publication to which the hon. member refers arose out of an incident which occurred as I was entering the chamber to make my speech yesterday. In reply to questions put to me by the lobby correspondent of the Star newspaper, I indicated to him the subject matter contained in the publication in question. I appreciate that this was a grave indiscretion on my part, for which I offer my deep apologies to the house.
This is the point: No real harm had been done to the state, because no knowledge had leaked out in time for fortunes to be made. But because there had been an appearance of indiscretion, the minister resigned. This was the principle involved. Let us compare those facts with the situation we have before us now in this house. I say again that it is the minister's responsibility; it is his decision. This is what Mr. Dalton said in his letter of resignation:
My dear Prime Minister,
In view of the incident which was raised today in the house I think it is my duty to offer you my resignation. If you accept it I shall continue, though now outside its ranks, to do my utmost to support the government-
He goes on to say he will continue to support the party. To that letter, the prime minister replied, expressing again the same old tradition in succinct words in the second paragraph:
I realize that this indiscretion in itself did not result in any action detrimental to the state, but the principle of the inviolability of the budget is of the highest importance and the discretion of ibe Chancellor of the Exchequer, who necessarily receives many confidential communications, must be beyond question.
Those were the feelings of the prime minister about the matter. Sir Winston Churchill had this to say:
In the circumstances we all regret that you have to resign but I must acknowledge with frankness that because of the indiscretion there was no alternative.


What was the result? The debate on the budget proceeded but a select committee was set up to inquire into the circumstances of the case. That committee made certain findings as to the facts. What were those findings? They were:
1.	Mr. Dalton made a premature and unpremeditated disclosure to Mr. Carvel of the contents of his budget, which disclosure he had no right to-make.
2.	Mr. Dalton did not make his disclosure for premature publication and believed there was no possibility of such publication.
3.	Mr. Carvel disclosed that information to his newspapers in the guise of a forecast, believing at the time that he was at liberty to do so. That belief was mistaken-
The report goes on to point out that no harm had been done to the state but that there had been an indiscretion.
I say, briefly, this: who are these people? What are the backgrounds of these people whose advice he sought? I say the minister has not only done harm to the economy of the country, he has not only upset confidence in financial circles but he has undermined his own people, because Mr. Harris is the majority owner of a millionaire company called Harris and Partners Ltd. I say the hon. gentleman is undermining the position of the Prime Minister himself. For who is Mr. Harris? He is married to a lady called Ethel Bowles who is first cousin to the Prime Minister. That is the spot on which the hon. gentleman has put his own leader. That is the spot on which he has put his own government. I say that the indiscretion here is far greater than anything that happened in the cases of Thomas and Dalton.
I could say the same about the expert who came from Wood, Gundy and Company. The basis for success in the government bond business is the ability to predict with some accuracy the future decisions of the government, because they affect tremendously the market. In making this statement nobody is implying dishonesty-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

I hear hon. members saying "Oh". Well, if they have other evidence let them come forward and tell the House of Commons. As I said, in making this statement no one is implying any dishonesty, but everything about these facts is contrary to traditions of budget secrecy here in Canada, as well as in the old country. The worst part is that whatever steps the government may take in the future, long after these experts have returned to advise their own firms, the suspicion always will be present in the public mind that both those firms have benefited.
I say that the indiscretion which has taken place in this case is the type of indiscretion

which should be examined by a select committee of the House of Commons where we could question witnesses and find out the facts. Members of the House of Commons are entitled to these facts. The people of Canada are entitled to them, because there has been some indiscretion.
Now I wish to deal with the contents of the budget itself.

Hard to believe that the new budget re sales tax on building materials can be of any use to our construction industry. It will create at least a 27 per cent drop in starts this year.
This is how this government intends to cure unemployment.

That telegram was from one of the officers of the building trade. One of the ministers-I think it was the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen)-said: We are going to be very gracious; we are going to pay upwards of $75 a month in certain circumstances. The hon. gentleman himself said the government intended to give everybody $500, who wished to build a house. But take ten per cent of $15,000, which is the average price of a new bungalow today. Make that calculation and hon. members will find the government has taken away $1,500. That is $1,000 benefit to the Department of National Revenue. And this is the kind of budget which was intended to help cure unemployment.
I said at the beginning that this government got to office not as a result of the last election but because of the fraud they perpetrated across the country on the issue of the pegging of the dollar and on the question of unemployment, as well as on account of another question which they added during the last campaign. We said: Canada for Canadians. We said: Canada should own its own industry. When we came forward with a program along those lines and took some imaginative steps in that regard, what did they say, those people who now sit on the government benches? They said:	Anti-
American. Well, they have learned now, the Americans, to beware of gifts and, sometimes

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those of us who are new members in this house I know are dismayed by the cynical attitude which some hon. members take toward the basic integrity and intelligence of other hon. members of the house. We have guilt by association. There is a fundamental lack of courtesy in recognizing that a man should not be judged guilty till he is proven guilty. We seem to lack the basic manners which the public at large expect of Canadians living together, and living democratically one with the other. I think epithets like "rogue" and "fool" are wrong and beneath the dignity not only of parliament but of the hon. members of parliament.
We are here tonight to discuss the budget and we have heard very little about the budget. We need to discuss the details, but before doing so we should have before us the findings of a national economic council, one which would show us basically where we have been and where we are going. We lack a good deal of that information now. We need to be able to agree on the facts, and having agreed on the facts we can then argue about the policies which we should adopt in order to correct the trends we see ahead of us.

The Budget-Mr. Davis In recent years we have had some wide swings in production and employment. We had in the late 40's and early 50's a very fortunate set of circumstances for this country. Our competitors abroad had been damaged by war. We did not have to compete as effectively then as we do now for our markets at home and elsewhere. We also had looking to this country, investors who were interested in raw materials for the industries, not only of the United States, but overseas. We had a tremendous amount of capital flowing into this country and it created a good deal of excess capacity. This excess capacity resulted in a slow down in investment in industry in the late 50's. Now we are witnessing some sort of upturn, perhaps towards a more normal state of affairs, but we are still investing only in the order of 22 per cent of our total output in new plant, equipment, buildings, homes and so on. A few years ago, in the middle 50's, this figure was more like 27 per cent. This is one of the fundamental reasons why employment has sagged in recent years and why unemployment will continue to be one of the most difficult problems we face in the years immediately ahead. Accompanying this sag in employment has been a drop in investment in industry. Industry which formerly invested as much as 17 per cent of our gross national product is down around 13 per cent.
The investment trends, particularly in respect of foreign ownership, are very important, and I should like to outline a few of them. Foreign ownership and control is a matter of great concern to those of us Canadians concerned with our survival as an independent political entity north of the 49th parallel. Here are some figures which come from an indisputable source, the dominion bureau of statistics. Direct foreign financing of our gross capital formation in this country rose from 19 per cent in the late 40's to 25 per cent in the early 50's, and has gone on to about 33 per cent in the late 50's. In other words, the participation of foreign investors in the growth of this country, in the installation of new plant and equipment, has been growing. It was large in the 40's, growing in the early 50's and has been increasing steadily ever since. We have witnessed in parallel an increasing foreign ownership of our manufacturing, mining and other basic industries. It has risen from the order of 55 per cent foreign ownership in 1944 to 61 per cent in 1957 and on to 63 per cent in 1959. I would venture to guess that perhaps two-thirds of the ownership and control of the industry of this country is now in the hands of people who do not normally reside within our borders. In other words, they own the most dynamic elements of our economy and the 
total amount of this ownership is in the vicinity of $25 billion. This is their book value.
If the assets were put on the auction block tomorrow they would undoubtedly fetch prices considerably in excess of this figure, perhaps $30 million, or more. This figure is in the order of magnitude of the total personal income of this country. In other words, every one of us would have to work for a year to buy out this foreign ownership. It is equal to something like $1,300 for every man, woman and child in the country, or more than $4,000 for every wage earner or salary earner in Canada. Obviously it will take us a long time to save up enough to buy out the foreigner, if we had the desire so to do. We have to set aside something in the order of $250 per year per wage earner in order merely to pay a reasonable rate of return on that investment, something in the order of 5 or 6 per cent. Many of these industries are capable of earning a good deal more, and therefore I suggest our annual bill in interest and dividends alone could well be upwards of $250 per person.
The character of this foreign ownership has changed to some degree. In this country it has largely taken a form of equity ownership, ownership which means real control over our destiny. It is not in the form of debt. It is not in the form of bonds, for example. It is not the type of financing done by foreigners in the early growth year of the United States. Even in the years immediately before world war I when the United States was still heavily dependant on the United Kingdom and western Europe, the great majority of the investment consisted of bonds, the fixed debt obligations paying fixed rates of interest and with a fixed life. As the lives of these bonds ended they were retired, and that indebtedness was extinguished.
This is not the type of indebtedness which we have in Canada today. In the last dozen years some 250 Canadian owned firms of substance have been bought out by residents of other countries. This tempo has been increasing. The rate at which these firms have been bought out has been doubled in the last half dozen years, compared to the rate for the previous six years. There has been an acceleration in this trend, and therefore it is a matter of some considerable concern to those Canadians who want to have some say in the destiny of this country, in the ownership of its resources, and more particularly in the management of the basic industrial activities which take place here.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not expect to be speaking for the full 30 minutes and would be glad to entertain a question at the end of my remarks. I do not want to infer that these outside investors have in any way been unfriendly to Canada. We have set the laws. We have set the ground rules. We have welcomed them in. They have invested in industries where they expected the industries to grow, where they expected them to pay dividends. We would certainly not be doing ourselves any good to reverse this attitude towards foreign ownership or foreign investment in this country.
However, foreign firms do not always behave precisely as do Canadian-owned firms. For example, while most foreign owned companies make tremendous contributions to every aspect of our life, particularly taxation, a few are not good citizens. One important area where these firms hurt us is in the service area. Insurance agents who have served a company for generations while it was Canadian-owned find the new foreign owner giving all his business to agencies outside the country. It is often found that these firms employ consulting engineers from, for example, a United States firm with whom they are familiar. Understandably they turn to these firms that they know. They turn to foreign firms to carry out market surveys, and foreign firms to do their advertising for them. All of these people are their friends and well known associates in other countries. This is not always to the good of Canada because it means that these foreign owned corporations tend to look abroad for services and for other things which, initially at least, we might expect them to find here in this country.
Then, too, in respect of charitable donations it is frequently found that foreign firms do not behave as Canadian firms do. Agencies which have long been dependant upon support of Canadian firms suddenly find this type of contribution for educational or other charitable purposes is not available for collection here.
The question now arises as to what we do about this situation. We can do nothing and allow the trend to continue towards even greater foreign ownership. Or we can release one of the great driving forces for socialization in this country. Governments, national, provincial or even municipal, could take over some of these activities. This was one of the main driving forces half a century ago, behind the formation of Ontario hydro. It is not exclusively a Canadian attitude towards foreign ownership. But, we have more government ownership and control of some industries 28902-5-90
The Budget-Mr. Davis because there is no other way to Canadianize industry or ensure that Canadians generally participate in their ownership and operation.
There is a Liberal answer as well to this question. It was foreshadowed by the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects back in 1957. I merely read a summary of the recommendations of that report. It is as follows:
1.	Wherever possible, such concerns-
-this is foreign-owned concerns-
-should employ Canadians in senior management and technical positions, should retain Canadian engineering and other professional and service personnel, and should do their purchasing of supplies, materials and equipment in this country:
2.	They should publish their financial statements and make full disclosure of the results of their Canadian operations;
3.	They should include on their boards of directors a number of independent Canadians and they should sell an appreciable interest in their equity stock to Canadians.
The commissioners said that they had in mind something of the order of 20 per cent to 25 per cent.
I should like to summarize the contents of the present budget which follow, quite logically and consistently from these recommendations of a half dozen years ago. I will itemize several of the most important:
1.	A withholding tax, a tax holdback on dividends. This is to be reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent for companies which are 25 per cent Canadian-owned. In other words, companies which are at least one quarter owned by Canadians do not have to pay as substantial a tax when the dividends are remitted out of the country as others which have a lesser extent of Canadian ownership.
2.	The withholding taxes on dividends to be increased to 20 per cent on January 1, 1965, for companies which are not 25 per cent Canadian-owned.
3.	Accelerated depreciation in areas of high unemployment, and only available to companies with at least 25 per cent Canadian ownership.
On the other side of the coin, and this applies to bonds, the withholding tax on interest is removed for non-taxable investors abroad. These are the basic considerations in the present budget.
Now, I should like to move on from foreign ownership and control, which I believe to be one of the principal elements of this budget and certainly an element which addresses itself to fundamental Canadian problems with which we have been living for some time, and about which we have done next to nothing, to certain other details of the budget.
In so far as the budget deficit is concerned, we have not been taxing to the extent

The Budget-Mr. Davis that we have been spending in this country. Our expenditures have, however, risen sharply. They have risen from roughly 26 per cent of our total national output in 1956 to something like 33 per cent currently. We will have, roughly, to match this increase in the proportion of our national wealth that comes back to the government in the form of taxes, or this vast budget deficit which we have continued to live with in recent years will grow with the passage of time. We will cause other people to lose faith in this country, to reduce their investments and cause simultaneously an increase in unemployment and a lack of confidence at home amongst Canadians.
One small item in the budget which I believe goes in the right direction is a reduction in the tax in respect of the export of electric power. This is of interest to me and to my province. I should like to focus on it for a moment. I concentrate on this tax because it is the one last remaining export taxes that is in effect in Canada. It has been in effect since 1925. Roughly speaking it amounted to about 10 per cent of the selling value of the power moving out of this country. It continued to be levied although the power was only circulated in and out of the country, out at one point and in at another, making a balance of the total amount in energy terms. The tax was merely applied to the outgoing amount. We need connections with adjoining areas to reduce the amount with standby capacity. This can account for a tremendous saving, and also could provide additional employment by actually providing power to the neighbouring areas of the United States.
I should like to indicate something of the magnitude of the power industry. Roughly 10 per cent of all the investment in this country, one out of ten of all the dollars that go into new construction goes into power plants and transmission lines. Some $5000 million of these assets exist in Canada today, but roughly $1,000 million worth of these facilities stand idle. We do not need all of this excess capacity to look after breakdowns or emergencies or exceptional upsurges in demand. We could get by with half as much. If we could sell the other half to the United States on a short term basis, this would currently return us something in the order of $50 million. Within six or seven years it could be $100 million. It could be a substantial item going towards balancing our presently unfavourable external account.
One item I hope to see in the budget next year is an extension of the concessions to research and development. Research and development is really the industry of ideas. It is the industry which, on this continent and elsewhere, has been growing far faster
[Mr. Davis.1
than the rest of the economy. It has doubled during the last five or six years. I believe we would do well in this country, because we have very little research, to declare Canada a tax heaven. In other words, the earnings, royalties, the yield on research and development, should be declared, for a substantial period of years at least, income tax free. This would cause firms not only at home but abroad to look upon Canada as a place in which to reduce costs, a place where they would encounter lower costs for research and development, and this would keep many of our own people at home. It would provide jobs for some of our younger people who expect exciting new job opportunities in fields like research which look ahead towards the shape of things to come. It would help us in respect of new products, in respect of cost cutting processes and would not only cause our economy to be better rounded but would also improve the efficiency of the industry we have here.
I think that even more important is the ownership aspect. When men are in a position of knowing what the forward thinking of a company or industry is in the area of research and development they are better able to invest more intelligently in the future of their company or firm. We do very little of this in Canada. We do about one fifth or one sixth as much as do the British and the Americans, and less still compared with West Germany and certain other countries. We must provide this sort of job opportunity for our people, both to give them the satisfaction of working in wonderful industries such as research and development and to improve the efficiency of our economy and to buy back some of the ownership in our own nation.
Finally, I should like to stress again that this budget, as I see it, has faced up to several substantial realities in Canada. One I have highlighted has been ownership and control. I think any other country would do the same. In fact, no other country in the world that I know of has done so little about this nagging and difficult problem of outside investment within their own country and particularly within the most dynamic segments of their industrial make-up.
In this government we are not anti-American and we are not anti-big business or antistock market. We are pro-Canadian and we are pro-enterprise, private and public. We are all for Canadians being able to buy more of the stocks in enterprises in this country, whether the majority of ownership is held outside of Canada or here. Confidence, I think, is the real key and Canadians fundamentally are a confident people. They want a little less talk and a little more action. I am sure they

want us here tonight to concentrate on the budget, on fundamental ideas in the budget and to take a positive attitude toward the future by being positive in our criticism and positive in our suggestions as to how to run the financial affairs of the country.

I shall not be presumptuous enough to say that the administration which I have supported for several years in this house has settled all economic problems in Canada. But we should never forget that the present government inherited a house in good order. Most of the basic indices of our economy were rising when the present government took over.
Under our administration, i.e., since 1956, the total increase in our exports of manufactured goods has reached 84.5 per cent. Second, the annual increase in living costs between 1958 and 1961 was 1.1 per cent, which means a smaller rise than in any other country in the world save one.

Those are the basic figures of a sound economic development.
Mr. Speaker, all hon. members will realize that for the welfare of our great young country, Canada, we should settle several problems as soon as possible, and pass legislation thereon. With that in my mind, 1 sincerely regret, with the whole Canadian people, that the speech the hon. Minister of Finance made before the house last Thursday night had such a partisan flavour. Indeed, his budget speech was one of the most partisan speeches ever made in this house by a minister of finance since confederation. His remarks, as I pointed out a few minutes ago, were full of partisan platitudes.
Once again, the leaders of the Liberal party are thinking that the welfare of their party is more important than the welfare of this country.

A few moments ago I said that I wanted to discuss one of the principles that is very close to the party I support in the House of Commons. Burke, one of the fathers of Conservative principle, had a high regard for the notion of "local self-agency." In Canada today this merely means that our federation only works when our provinces, cities, towns and municipalities are strong and able to carry out their constitutional responsibilities.
When the party I support in this house came to power in 1957, total federal contributions and payments to all provinces amounted to $689,352,000 for the fiscal year 1956-57. In the year 1962-63, for the same purposes, the figure amounted to $1,794,061,000. At the same time I fully realize that many problems touching upon federal-provincial affairs remain to be solved. To this end I wish to discuss the federal-provincial relations section of the budget. Hon. members opposite on the treasury

benches are burying their heads in the sand if they do not realize that a healthy confederation and a healthy spirit of biculturalism will only continue if the Minister of Finance understands that the taxing powers of the provinces mean a lot. I am sure he not only got no outside advice in relation to the federal-provincial relations section of his budget, but that he got no advice at all.
It was with great dismay I noticed the apparent lack of understanding by the Minister of Finance of some basic issues which face our people today within the general framework of the question of federal-provincial relations and biculturalism. During the past election campaign the Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec got together. I am not quite sure what they talked about. It must have been about something; and then we were told in Quebec that in order to save confederation all we had to do was elect Liberal governments in Ottawa and Quebec. But, Mr. Speaker, what have we seen since a Liberal government has taken office here in Ottawa? On the one hand they talk of co-operative federalism, while on the other hand their throne speech and plans indicate a degree of centralization unprecedented in the history of Canada. Intricate legislation, such as loans to municipalities, was proposed and, after continued questioning of the ministry, we learned that none of the provinces was consulted in general or specific terms. While provincial premiers speak out for a thorough re-examination of our constitutional approach, the budget clearly demonstrates that unless the federal government acts immediately, and not tomorrow, the provinces will be faced with a fait accompli at the next federal-provincial conference whenever it is decided to be held.
Liberal spokesmen have created by their campaign tactics a high degree of expectancy in this house. One program in Quebec, another program in the rest of Canada; they have been at their old game. I suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) turns around and faces Mr. Lesage and the other ten provincial premiers. After sitting in this house for a number of weeks and after hearing, especially, the budget address, it has become apparent to me and it is my firm belief that the problem of federal-provincial relations and biculturalism has received no serious thought on the part of the present government. New, not old, approaches must be used and many of the problems, sir, cannot wait for the findings of royal commissions. We were criticized, when we were in office, when we set up royal commissions. This government is now setting up a royal commission for one of the most important problems that is facing Canada today. I see

It is a phrase that hon. members opposite think they initiated. But the motion of co-operative federalism constitutes by no means a novel approach. If such were the case, no longer would the federal authority propose legislation involving the provinces without prior consultation; no longer would the provincial

The Budget-Mr. Grafftey and federal governments approach the summit of federal-provincial conferences at opposite ends of the pole without previous attempts at negotiating points of view and without any basic consultation since the last conference. Fiscal relations are at the heart of many of the problems facing the healthy continuance of our federal union, and true biculturalism. Immediate changes are imperative.

Such a secretariat would increase the efficiency of separated powers, whether exercised alone or in a common endeavour. speechtext:
When we consider that economic factors never seemed to be the most important considerations which contributed to confederation in the first place, such a proposal for the establishment today of a federal-provincial permanent secretariat, when economic and fiscal matters are of such great importance, is of such vital concern to my way of thinking and to the way of thinking of many hon. members, that it must be acted upon immediately.
Not long ago, when the provincial premiers met in Victoria, British Columbia, Premier Lesage of Quebec mentioned the strong possibility that the provinces might join together to form their own permanent secretariat. He noted that many areas require co-operation simply among the provinces themselves, without mentioning the necessity for co-operation among the provinces and the federal government. This is most notable, perhaps, in the resources field. The first steps to be taken seem to involve the immediate necessity for the provinces and the federal government to set up their respective general secretariats. We need not fear the idea of competing secretariats if we carry the whole idea one


step further and look at progress already made with the joint national resources council which came into being under the last administration. This was the first concept of true co-operative federalism.
All provinces, under this system, and the federal government are represented and we see here the idea of a super-provincial-federal organization. Nothing is imposed on the provinces. They are never presented with a fait accompli. Working formulas are negotiated and evolved on a continuing basis. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this concept must be widened to include at least fiscal arrangements. Perhaps there are those who feel the provinces and the federal government should not set up separate secretariats before one general joint secretariat is set up. For this reason I have purposefully not entered into details. On the other hand, I do hope these broad proposals may play some small part- I am addressing these words to the Minister of Finance-in solving a problem which Canadians of all political parties fully realize must be dealt with immediately. The Minister of Finance of this Liberal party would not, I am sure, be too pleased if he saw the behaviour of his party in the province of Quebec. But the province of Quebec, with the other provinces, wants action now because of the way the Liberals behaved during the election campaign. This is the party that was going to save confederation. Therefore I say to the government, show the people of Quebec and all provinces of Canada your good faith.
With the people of my province, Mr. Speaker, I am optimistic about the future of confederation. Yet I am a realistic optimist, and realism dictates that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues indicate that they are doing some positive thinking and are ready to act. Such an approach to the question of dominion-provincial relations and to the question of biculturalism will help to ensure that 1967 will be a true celebration for all the provinces of Canada and for all Canadians.

speechtext:
Wait for it, boys; we are coming to the subject. I feel sure we all acknowledge that the stand taken by the minister with regard to cigarette smoking has been motivated only by her keen and sincere concern for the future health of the youth of this country. I think we must all commend her for her ideas in that direction. It is not my intention in any way to dispute the findings of the medical authorities. But I want to say this: if the medical authorities are truly sincere in their efforts to protect the health of this nation, they had better take a really long look in some other directions and at some other products. Let us take one such product, for example, tranquillizers. Tranquillizers are being used today not only by adults but increasingly by the youth of our nation. I think hon. members will have to realize that these drugs are going a long way towards breaking down the mental and moral health of our young people.
Then, of course, there is that likeable and friendly old fellow, old John Barleycorn. In fact, I like to get friendly with him once in a while. And when I talk about friendly old John I hope the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) will not think I am referring to him. I would like to take dear old John and cut him up into three pieces. The first one has to do with health. I think everyone knows that there is a great deal of evidence about the effect of dear old John on the health of the nation in more ways than one. Indeed, medical men are beginning to think of too great an indulgence in alcohol as being a disease. They are actually contemplating putting up institutions to handle people suffering from this disease. This is where the comparison with tobacco comes in. I think that if comparable experiments were made the adverse effects on health caused by dear old John would easily outweigh those of tobacco.
Then there is the effect of alcohol in relation to our mental institutions. I often wonder whether the medical authorities know anything about the mental institutions which exist in the Dominion of Canada today. I am not blaming dear old John for putting the majority of the present inmates into these institutions, but I think every hon. member here will realize that he is responsible for a great number of these people finding themselves in institutions.
Then there is the moral angle. There are the broken homes. Let us face the fact that the effects of too much alcohol go a long way towards breaking down the moral fibre of this
The Budget-Mr. Roxburgh country. Again, I should like to say that if the medical men in Canada want to take a look at some of these things they had better take a long, hard look at some of these other products, because the tobacco situation is nothing but peanuts compared with them.
We grow it in good old Norfolk county- between $40 millions and $50 millions worth. Tobacco in Ontario today is a multi-million dollar business. It is an established business and a proven business. Are we going to sell it down the drain? I should like to bring a few facts to the attention of hon. members. I know they will smile when I refer to a certain product and compare it with tobacco. Believe it or not, that product is wheat, and wheat is the lifeblood of Canada, grown of course by those great farmers out in western Canada. Wheat returns to those farmers something like $500 million a year, but even so the government has to subsidize the wheat growers of western Canada through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, through grants in respect of unharvested crops, acreage payments, storage payments, and so on to the tune of about $100 million a year. The tobacco industry returns to the growers of Ontario around $100 million a year. It has returned to the government by way of excise duty and taxes hundreds of millions of dollars over the years. On the average it returns every year approximately $400 million in taxes. This is derived from somewhere between 120 to 130 thousand acres of land in Ontario. This area produces the highest grade tobacco in the world. Hon. members will say it is a new industry, 35 to 40 years of age. But any new industry needs help from older industries, and from the United States came the boys from North and South Carolina and other places, and they taught us how to grow tobacco. When the season was over they went back to their homes in the Carolinas and Virginia, taking with them hands of tobacco grown in Ontario. What did they do with those hands of tobacco? They thought they would have a little fun and gave them to their relatives and friends to enter as exhibits in tobacco shows in the United States. And what happened? They just walked away with the prizes.
Mr Speaker, this is an industry that has not been living out of the pockets of the country. Tobacco growing is an industry which has been putting money back into the country's pockets, not taking it out like some other industries within the dominion. If ever there was an industry which needs adjustment assistance and help in the research field, it is the tobacco industry. I am sure every hon. member here will agree that this industry has earned its right to expect some help, because as I say, for years it has been

The Budget-Mr. Roxburgh pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the pockets of Canada to help keep other industries going ahead. Are we going to kill an industry? Are we going to cut the head off the goose that laid the golden egg?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Good. I realize there has been a lot of unwarranted publicity given to this subject recently. Suggestions have been made that programs are to be worked out to reduce or even eliminate the habit of smoking cigarettes. If such is really the case then this government should take a forward step in stopping expansion of the tobacco industry and leave it where it is now. It is a stabilized industry, and if this obnoxious weed is so obnoxious and if these statements are correct, as I expect they are, then its growth should go no further and the people responsible for the industry and who have invested money should be protected. The government of the day should give certain protection to this industry, which has proven itself. This could be done by making a sincere effort to bring about national marketing board legislation. This should not be delayed. I think we all realize it cannot be done without the co-operation of the provinces. That is also true of portable pensions, contributory old age pensions and so on, and I know the present government will take immediate steps to put this legislation before the house. I ask the present government to do this on behalf of a $100 million business returning, as I say, $400 million a year to the government in tax.
A substantial effort should also be made to export this product. Many hon. members will smile and say that it has been tried but we have not had very much luck. The United States has already put forward ideas to expand their export trade. We have some of our own which we intend to carry out, but we can always learn from others. I think one of the best ideas which has come across the line is this. They have employed men- call them, if you like, good relations officers- who are sent to countries to which the United States exports a great deal. They work in conjunction with the United States embassy, and when any product, whether it be tobacco, machinery, or what have you, is exported to that country they are there to give advice. Suppose we export tobacco to a country and it does not arrive there in the condition it should. Naturally the importer is perturbed and will not pay the price. Or suppose for some reason or other the product is in good condition but the importer thinks he can pull a fast one and says it has not arrived in good condition. The men employed by the United States would follow up such a complaint. If it concerned an export from that country they would talk


things over. This would bring them closer together and get them to forget their differences. The United States has proven that by this method they have not only kept their export trade but have increased it.
The hon. members may ask what are the possibilities of exports? A lot of people say it is no use going to a different country to export because the United States exports to that country, or somebody else does. Well, if we all took that attitude no new industry would start up either in this or any other country. Speaking as a fruit grower, when we have a large crop of apples or peaches, or whatever it may be, if we sat on our fannies all the time we certainly would not sell very much fruit. We have to get out and work for it.
Now, I should like to point out to you that Great Britain imports from Canada 11 per cent, from the United States 50 per cent. Belgium imports from Canada one third of 1 per cent, and 28 per cent from the United States. West Germany imports 1 per cent from Canada, and 40 per cent from the United States, and so on. One could go on so far as this part is concerned, and talk about this industry and the return it has made to this country in the form of taxes. We can, without taking one cent in the form of taxes from any other product, take some of the $400 million to help this industry while it is fighting for its life. After all, this is an industry that has poured money into the governments of Canada for the last number of years. We can spend money for experimental purposes. We can spend money for marketing. We can spend money for research in the interests of the tobacco industry. This money will come from the tobacco industry itself.
I know that a number of salesmen and other people will say that the subsidies paid by the United States government represent the reason their tobacco is selling overseas and ours is not. I know that at the mention of subsidies everybody will throw up their hands and say, "Oh, not another subsidy for an agricultural product". I should like to say to my hon. friends opposite that this money can be taken from the industry itself. Surely an industry that has poured the money into our pockets that this industry has over the years deserves some consideration. We are not asking that money should come from any other product to help subsidize us. Surely* we can use some of this money to subsidize the industry now.
In summing up, I should like to say that I think one of the most important factors is to stop further expansion of tobacco growing. I should like to repeat that tobacco farmers in Ontario produce 99.9 per cent of the tobacco Canada uses. If all these facts that

the medical profession claim are true, and I am not denying them, then why should this or any other government allow the Farm Credit Corporation and other corporations to lend money to people to grow more tobacco? It just is not sensible. We have all we need at the present time. In other words, the present tobacco farm marketing board is being backed to the tune of millions of dollars to try to help sell this surplus tobacco.
Then, there should be a subsidy given for assistance in research. Here is an industry which, if it is not looked after, not given just a little bit of help, might go down the drain. No one is saying that in five months or five years the research people will not make it possible for everybody to continue to smoke cigarettes without any detriment. In my opinion it might be possible for the Department of Trade and Commerce to have people work through the embassies to sell our tobacco.
Let me point out again, Mr. Speaker, that this is a proven business, a business that is going to need some form of protection while it adjusts itself to the new problem facing it today. In my opinion at least, it is only good common sense that such a business should be protected because, in the long run, it is going to return millions of dollars to governments now and in the future, and is going to be of value in other ways and do more good than we will ever realize.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in joining in this debate I must first of all congratulate you on your appointment as Deputy Speaker. Of course, I must congratulate the Speaker as well. This traditional honour, I think, falls on very worthy shoulders. Before commencing my remarks this evening I must say that I have been a friend of the Speaker for some time. He was one of those who assisted me when I first came here in 1957.
I want to make my remarks on the budget under three main headings this evening. The first one is the tax incentives as they are applicable to northern development. The second is the budget as it applies or does not apply to the mining economy of the north. Third, I want to state some facts for the record in connection with the Dawson city festival which has received so much lampooning and so many unkind remarks from the government side of the house.
Before doing this, however, I want to comment very briefly on the manner in which this budget was prepared. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the charges that were levelled at the former government now the official opposition, last year and the year before in connection with fumbling and bumbling, in connection with lack of decision, are applicable now with more force 28902-5-91
The Budget-Mr. Nielsen than ever to the members of the treasury benches. This is particularly true when one views the panic into which the stock exchanges of this country were thrown as a result of the premature announcement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) yesterday.
Another thing upon which I should like to comment before going into the matter of the budget as it affects northern development, is the question of tax incentives about which the Minister of Finance had written for so long, and which the Liberal government had promised for so long for the encouragement and development of industry in Canada. Representations have been made for a long time to the government, to the officials of the Department of Finance, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, to northern affairs and national resources, to the effect that new mines in the north should be granted an increased tax exempt period. As we all know this period is three years for new mines. This is not enough. Over the past decade representations have been made repeatedly that this exempt period should be increased to at least five years. Out of the Northwest Territories Council have come resolutions to this effect. Out of the northern resources conference in Edmonton and from the associated boards of trade of the Pacific northwest meeting in Whitehorse has come the same sort of recommendation.
We do not see any mention of this in the budget, and this is supposed to be a budget to induce the development of Canada's resources and to induce the development of secondary industry. So it would appear that the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Benidickson) either is not familiar with the problems that confront the mining industry and has not impressed upon his colleagues the need for this added incentive in the north, or his representations have had no effect on the Minister of Finance. In this regard, when I speak of the north I do not mean merely the north above the 60th parallel but the northern portion of Canada which comprises about 80 per cent of the nation.
I think the same observation can be made pretty well with regard to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) because certainly he has had sufficient time now to have become familiar with the problems of the north. He has made a visit there and I have no doubt he has spoken to many people in the mining industry. As a matter of fact, he has made speeches in this connection. Yet even his influence has had no effect in impressing the Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Nielsen Finance with the need for this type of incentive for the development of the mining industry in the north.
When this country was developing from east to west it was the resources of the west that finally made that contribution to national development which made the west what it is today. If the Minister of Finance and his colleagues, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, had projected their thoughts in the creation of the budget along the same line of thinking that made for success in Sir John A. Macdonald's time, we might have had more incentive to encourage risk capital to go into the north for the purpose of developing the resources there.
Many people have no idea just how extensive the resources of the north are. If I were to tell hon. members that in the Yukon river basin alone there is a potential of 50 billion kilowatt hours of hydroelectric power and contrasted that with the total potential of the nation, it might impress them. If I were to say also that the oil and gas reserves in Canada above the 60th parallel total 50 billion barrels compared with 4.77 billion for the known reserves in the rest of Canada surely that might be some ground for the Minister of Finance to offer these incentives to the development of Canadian resources in the north.
I intend to say a word or two about the mining economy of the north a little later in my remarks, but I will pass now to the question of directing people into developing the industry of the north from the point of view of the budget that the Minister of Finance has presented. Along with the representations that have been made for tax incentives to the mining industry that would develop industry in the north, there have been hand in hand representations made by several organizations, both industrial and labour, for an increased personal tax exemption in the north. As recently as last year a delegation from the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers presented a brief to several members of the cabinet calling for an increase in the basic income tax exemption of individuals in the north to help to compensate for the higher cost of living there.
Obviously the government recognizes the principle that it is desirable to offset the difference between the cost of living in the north and that in the more southerly portions of Canada. They do this by offering what are known as isolated post allowances to civil servants who are required to go to the north for the purpose of discharging their respon-

sibilities and duties. Isolated post allowances vary from a maximum of $2,600 a year for a married man who happens to be stationed in the more remote areas of Canada's north, such as Alert, to a low of $750 for a single man who happens to be posted in any area of northern Canada. Again I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that in this sense northern Canada includes those portions of northern Canada below the 60th parallel.
The government does this for the purpose of compensating the civil servant for the difference in the cost of living between that experienced by him if he performs his functions in the south and the cost of living in northern Canada. If it is a right principle to offer civil servants a cost of living bonus, which in essence is what it is, in the form of isolated post allowances, then the organizations that have made these representations to the government from time to time feel that it is just as right in principle that some sort of compensation should be offered to other citizens in the north in order to assist settlement in northern Canada and in order to eliminate what amounts to a discriminatory fiscal measure which is applicable only to civil servants and not to ordinary citizens in the north.
The government of Canada, which subsidizes wages for its civil servants through isolated post allowances because of the high cost of living in the north, should make provision for income tax allowances for other citizens. Representations have been made several times in this regard and I am rather surprised that the Minister of Finance has so forgotten Canadian citizens in the north as to have overlooked these representations, or even mention of them. Just as the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces and territories build roads to facilitate industry, which has been carried on in the last six years to a degree that has brought about development of resources in the north, and in the northern portions of the provinces, more than at any other time in Canada's history, there should be special recognition of this factor of the higher cost of living. We propose that it should be done by granting to all taxpayers in the Yukon and Northwest Territories an increased basic exemption, and if not based on a formula comparable to that used in calculating isolated post allowances then it should be on a flat rate.
